title: A prayer as the eighth book begins
english: I have now come to the end of seven books, and I wish to begin an eighth. God and His “only-begotten” Word (John 1:14) will be present with us, so that the falsehoods of Celsus, which he has vainly entitled The True Doctrine, may be nobly refuted, and so that the teachings of Christianity may be powerfully demonstrated, as far as this lies in what is being dictated. We pray that, with the mind of Paul, we may say, “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us” (2 Corinthians 5:20), and that we may be ambassadors “for Christ” to men, just as the Word of God calls them to friendship with Himself, since He wishes to bring into kinship with righteousness and truth and the other virtues those who, before they received the teachings of Jesus the Christ, had spent their lives in darkness about God and in ignorance of the Creator.

And again I will say: may God grant us the noble and true Word, the Lord strong and mighty “in battle” (Psalm 24:8) against wickedness. Now we must go on to the next passage of Celsus and to what is to be said against it.

title: Celsus on serving more than one master
english: In what came before, he raised the question against us why we do not worship demons; and we answered what he said about demons according to what seemed to us the intent of the divine word. Then, next after that, he brings us in as saying, in answer to his question, since he wants us to worship the demons too, that the same man cannot “serve” several “masters” (Matthew 6:24). This, he thinks, is the voice of sedition, the voice of those who, as he himself called them, “wall themselves off and break away from the rest of mankind.” He supposes that those who say this are, as far as in them lies, projecting their own passion onto God.

That is why he thinks it holds good among men that one who serves someone could not reasonably “serve” another man too, since one of the two would be harmed by the divided service; and that one who has already sworn alliance with someone should not swear alliance with another as well, since that would harm the first; and that it is reasonable not to serve at the same time various heroes and demons of that kind. But in the case of God, whom neither harm nor grief can reach, he thinks it unreasonable to guard against worshipping several gods, as one does in matters concerning men and heroes and demons of this kind. He also says that the one who worships several gods, by worshipping some one of the beings that belong to the great God, in this too does what is dear to Him; and he adds that no one may be honoured to whom this has not been given by Him. “Therefore,” he says, “one who honours and reverences all who are His does not grieve God, to whom they all belong.”

title: The gods whom Scripture knows
english: Before we go on to what follows, let us see whether we are not right to accept the saying, “No one can serve two masters,” to which is added, “for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other,” and next to it, “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24). Our defence calls us to a deeper and secret teaching about gods and lords.

For the divine Scripture knows that the Lord is great above “all the gods” (Psalm 135:5). By “gods” here we do not understand those worshipped among the nations, since we have learned that “all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5). We understand “gods” of whom the prophetic word knows a certain assembly, with the God over all judging between them and assigning to each the work proper to him. For “God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst He will judge between gods” (Psalm 82:1). For He is also “the God of gods, the Lord,” who through the Son “called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Psalm 50:1). And we are commanded to give thanks “to the God of gods” (Psalm 136:2), having also learned that “God is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). These things are said not only through the passages set out here but through countless others.

title: For us one God and one Lord
english: Such, too, are the things that the divine words teach us to examine and to hold about the Lord and lords. In one place they say: “Give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy is for ever; give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy is for ever” (Psalm 136:2–3); in another, that God is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). The word knows of gods, some of whom are so called, while others actually are gods, whether they are so called or not. Paul teaches the same about lords too, both those who are and those who are not, when he says: “For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5).

Then, since “the God of gods” calls “from the east” and “the west” (Psalm 50:1; Matthew 8:11) into His own portion, through Jesus, those whom He wills, and since the Christ of God, being Lord, shows that He surpasses all who hold lordship by the very fact that He has set foot within the borders of all and calls to Himself from every border, for this reason Paul, knowing these things, says after the words I have quoted: “yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through Him” (1 Corinthians 8:6). And seeing a wonderful and mysterious teaching in the passage, he adds to these words: “But not all have this knowledge” (1 Corinthians 8:7).

When he says, “yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6), he says “for us” of himself and of all who have ascended to the God over all, the God “of gods,” and to the Lord over all, the Lord “of lords.” And the one who has ascended to the God over all is he who worships Him without division, without separation, without partition, through the Son, God’s Word and Wisdom seen in Jesus, who alone brings to Him those who try in every way, by excellent words and deeds and thoughts, to bring themselves into kinship with God, the Maker of the universe.

Over against these truths, and others like them, I think that the ruler “of this age” (1 Corinthians 2:6), who disguises himself “as an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14), produced the saying: “And there follows him a host of gods and demons, marshalled in eleven companies” (Plato, Phaedrus 246e). In this passage he says of himself and of those who have practised philosophy: “We with Zeus, and others with other demons” (Plato, Phaedrus 250b).

title: Rising above every other master
english: Since, then, there are many gods, whether so called or real, and likewise many lords, we do all we can to rise above not only the things worshipped as gods among the nations on earth, but also those whom the Scriptures call gods. About these they know nothing who are “strangers to the covenants” (Ephesians 2:12) of God given through Moses and through our Saviour Jesus, and who are aliens to His promises made known through these.

The one who does no work that is dear to demons rises above servitude to all demons. And the one who looks “not to the things that are seen but to the things that are not seen” (2 Corinthians 4:18), whether in the way those beings do or however the matter may stand, rises above the portion of those whom Paul says are gods. And when a man sees how “the eager longing of the creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19), “not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it, in hope” (Romans 8:20); when he speaks of the creation with reverence and sees how all of it “will be set free from its bondage to corruption” and will come “into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21), he is not drawn away into serving God and some other being along with Him, nor into “serving two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

So it is not the voice of sedition in those who have understood such things and do not wish to “serve” several “masters,” and who for this reason are content with the Lord Jesus Christ. He trains under Himself those who serve Him, so that, when they have been trained and have become a “kingdom” worthy of God, He may hand them over to God the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24). Yet they do cut themselves off and break away from those who are aliens to “the commonwealth” of God and strangers to His “covenants” (Ephesians 2:12), so that they may live as citizens of “the commonwealth in heaven” (Philippians 3:20), drawing near to the living God “and to the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Hebrews 12:22–23).

title: Ambassadors who will not bow
english: Nor is it as though God were harmed, as a man seems to be harmed by one who also serves another besides him, that we refuse to serve any other than God, through His Word and His Truth. It is so that we may not harm ourselves by separating ourselves from the portion of the God over all, since we live in kinship with His blessedness by the excellent “spirit of adoption.” That spirit is in the sons of the Father in heaven, who cry aloud in secret “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15), uttering not mere words but realities.

The ambassadors of the Lacedaemonians, though the king’s bodyguards pressed them hard, did not bow down before the king of the Persians, because they feared their one lord, the law of Lycurgus (Herodotus, Histories 7.136). But those who go on the far greater and more divine embassy “for Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:20) would not bow down before the ruler of the Persians, or of the Greeks, or of the Egyptians, or of any nation whatever, even if the bodyguards of those rulers, demons and angels of the devil, should wish to force them to do so, and should try to persuade them to say a long farewell to Him who is greater than every law on earth. For the Lord of those who are ambassadors “for Christ” is Christ, for whom they are ambassadors, who was the Word “in the beginning,” who was “with God,” and who was “God” (John 1:1).

title: What harm can heroes suffer?
english: Next, Celsus seemed to be stirring up an argument about heroes and certain demons that went deeper than he could see. For after his argument about service to men, in which the first master, whom someone wishes to serve, is harmed if he also wishes to serve a second, he says that “the same would hold also for heroes and for demons of this kind.” We must ask him what he means by heroes, and of what sort he says these demons are, such that the one who serves this hero must not serve another, and the one who serves this demon must not serve another as well, as though the first demons, whom someone worshipped before the second, were harmed in the same way as men are harmed. Let him also show what harm he thinks heroes or such demons suffer. For either he will fall into a sea of nonsense and be forced to take back his argument and reject what he has said, or, if he does not wish to talk nonsense, he will be forced to admit that he knows neither heroes nor the nature of demons.

And to his argument about men, that the first are harmed if someone serves a second, we must reply: what kind of harm does he say comes to the first man, if the one who serves him wishes to serve another as well?

title: No harm can touch the wise
english: For if he were to speak as a layman and, in an unphilosophical way, take harm to mean harm to possessions, the things called external to us, he would be refuted as one who had not even paid attention to the fine saying of Socrates: “Anytus and Meletus can kill me, but they cannot harm me; for it is not permitted that the better should be harmed by the worse” (Plato, Apology 30c-d). And if by harm he means a movement or a state that accords with vice, it is clear that when a man serves two wise men who live in different places, no harm at all comes to the wise. But if not even this is reasonable, then it is in vain that he has taken up the example as a charge against the saying “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). And all the more will the argument prevail for serving the God of the universe alone, through His Son, who brings us to God.

Moreover, we will worship God not as though He were in need, nor as though He were grieved if we do not worship Him, but because we ourselves are helped by the worship of God, and because we become free from grief and from passion by serving the God over all through His only-begotten Word and Wisdom.

title: Who grants the right to be honoured
english: See how ill-considered are the words “For if you also worship anything else in the universe”, which imply that the worship of God carries us on, without any harm to ourselves, to any one of the things that belong to God, without distinction. But as if he had noticed that he had not spoken soundly in saying “For if you also worship anything else in the universe”, he takes the point up again and corrects his statement with these words: “Nor may anyone be honoured to whom this has not been granted by Him.”

So let us ask Celsus about those who are honoured as gods, or demons, or even heroes: On what grounds, my good man, can you prove that the right to be honoured was granted to them by God, and not by the ignorance and want of learning of human beings who wander and fall away from the One to whom honour properly belongs? Hadrian’s favourite, at any rate, is honoured, as you said a little while ago, Celsus; and surely you will not say that it was the God of the universe who granted Antinous the right to be honoured as a god. We will say the same about the others too, and demand proof that the right to be honoured was granted to them by the God who is over all.

But if he turns a similar objection back on us concerning Jesus, we will show that it was from God that the right to be honoured was granted to Him: “that all may honour the Son, just as they honour the Father” (John 5:23). For the prophecies made before His birth were the credentials of His honour. And the wonders He worked, not by sorcery, as Celsus supposes, but by a divine power foretold by the prophets, had their testimony from God, so that whoever “honours the Son” (John 5:23), who is the Word, does nothing contrary to reason and may be benefited by honouring Him; and that, honouring Him who is the Truth (John 14:6), he may become better through honouring truth, and in the same way through honouring wisdom and righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and all the things that the divine Scriptures say the Son of God is.

title: Honour shown by a sound life
english: See whether we are not taught that honour toward the Son of God, and in the same way honour toward God the Father, is rendered through a sound life, both from the words “You who boast in the law dishonour God by breaking the law” (Romans 2:23), and from these: “How much worse a punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has counted as common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Hebrews 10:29). For if the one who breaks the law dishonours God “by breaking the law” (Romans 2:23), and the one who tramples on the Word tramples underfoot “the Son of God” (Hebrews 10:29), it is plain that the one who keeps the law honours God, and the one who is adorned with the Word of God and with His works reveres God.

If Celsus had known who belong to God, namely the wise alone, and who are strangers to Him, namely all the wicked who show no inclination at all to take up virtue, he would have seen in what sense one ought to say his words: “If then one honours and reveres all who are His, how does he grieve God, to whom they all belong?”

title: No faction in the kingdom of God
english: Next after this he says: “And yet the one who, speaking about God, asserts that one Lord is meant is impious, because he divides the kingdom of God and creates faction, as though there were a party, and some other rival opposed to Him.”

This would have had some force for him if he had proved by geometrical demonstrations that those whom the nations worship as gods really are gods, and had shown that those who are believed to dwell about statues and temples and altars are not some wicked demons. But as for the kingdom of God, which is constantly spoken of and written about among us, we pray both to understand it and to become such that we may be ruled by God alone, and that the kingdom of God may become ours also. He, on the other hand, who teaches us to revere many gods, ought, if he looks at what follows from his own position, to speak of a kingdom of gods rather than of God.

So there are no factions with God, nor is there any god who is His rival, even if some, like Giants or Titans, wish through their own wickedness to fight against God, together with Celsus and those who have taken up war against Him who in countless ways established what concerns Jesus, and against Jesus Himself, who for the salvation of our race gave Himself, being the Word, to the whole world at once, as each is able to receive Him.

title: One God, the Father and the Son
english: Next, he might seem to say something plausible against us in these words: “If these people worshipped no other but one God, they would perhaps have a strong argument against the others. But as it is, they worship beyond measure this man who appeared only lately, and yet they think they commit no offence against God if His servant also is worshipped.”

To this too we must reply that, if Celsus had understood the words “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and those spoken in prayer by the Son of God, “as I and You are one” (John 17:22), he would not have supposed that we worship any other besides the God who is over all. For “the Father”, He says, “is in me, and I in the Father” (John 10:38). But if anyone is troubled by these words, fearing that we may somehow be going over to those who deny that the Father and the Son are two distinct realities, let him attend to the words “the heart and soul of all who believed were one” (Acts 4:32), so that he may understand “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). So, as we have explained, we worship one God, the Father and the Son.

And our strong argument against the others still holds; nor do we worship beyond measure one who appeared only lately, as though He had not existed before. For we believe Him who said, “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58), and who says, “I am the Truth” (John 14:6). And none of us is so servile in mind as to think that the being of truth did not exist before the time when Christ appeared. We worship, then, the Father of the Truth and the Son who is the Truth, two realities in their distinct existence, but one in unity of mind, in harmony, and in sameness of will. So the one who has seen the Son, who is “the radiance of the glory” and the imprint “of the being” of God (Hebrews 1:3), has seen God in Him (John 14:9), since He is the image of God (Colossians 1:15).

title: Which servants of God we worship
english: Then he thinks that, because we worship His Son together with God, it follows for us that on our own view not only God but also His servants are to be worshipped. Now if he had meant those who are truly servants of God after the Only-begotten of God, Gabriel and Michael and the rest of the angels, and had said that these ought to be worshipped, then perhaps, after clearing up what he means by worship and what acts the worshipper performs, we would have said on the subject, as men discussing matters so great, whatever we were able to understand about them. But as it is, since he takes as God’s servants the demons whom the nations worship, he does not bind us by any logic to worship such beings; for our teaching shows them to be servants of the evil one, and of the ruler of this age (John 12:31; 1 Corinthians 2:6), who draws away from God whomever he can.

So it is because they are not God’s servants that we refuse to revere and worship all those whom the rest of mankind reveres; for had we been taught that they were servants of the God who is over all, we would not call them demons. Therefore we revere the one God and His one Son, His Word and Image, with supplications and petitions as far as we are able, bringing our prayers to the God of the universe through His Only-begotten. To Him we first offer them, and we ask Him, who is “the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2), to bring our prayers and sacrifices and intercessions as High Priest (Hebrews 2:17) to the God who is over all.

Our faith, then, is directed to God through His Son, who confirms it in us; and Celsus can show no faction of ours concerning the Son of God. And we do revere the Father, as we admire His Son, the Word and Wisdom and Truth and Righteousness, and all that we have learned the Son of God to be; and so we revere also Him who was begotten of such a Father. So much for this.

title: The founder of peace, not faction
english: Celsus says again: “If you were to teach them that this man is not His child, but that He is the Father of all, who alone ought truly to be revered, they would no longer be willing, unless they were to revere this man too, who is the founder of their faction. And they called him Son of God not because they revere God greatly, but because they exalt this man greatly.”

We, however, have learned who the Son of God is: that He is “the radiance of the glory and the imprint of His being” (Hebrews 1:3), and “a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25), and again “the radiance of eternal light, and a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of His goodness” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). So we know that He is the Son who comes from God, and that God is His Father. And there is nothing unseemly in this teaching, nor anything unfitting for God, who gives existence to such an only-begotten Son. No one could persuade us that such a one is not the Son of the unbegotten God and Father. If Celsus has heard some people who do not confess that the Son of God is the Son of the One who made this universe, that is a matter for him and for those who agree with such teaching.

Jesus, then, is the founder not of faction but of all peace. He said to the disciples, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27). Then, since He knew that men of the world and not of God would make war on us, He added to those words, “Not as the world gives peace do I give you peace” (John 14:27). And even if we are afflicted in the world, we take courage because of Him who said, “In the world you have affliction; but take courage, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

He is the One we say is the Son of God; of God, whom, if we must follow Celsus’s wording, we revere greatly; and we know that His Son has been greatly exalted by the Father. Grant that some, as may happen in a multitude of believers who admit differences of opinion, rashly suppose that the Saviour is the supreme God over all. We do not; for we obey Him when He says, “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28). That is why we would not subject Him whom we now call Father to the Son of God, as Celsus falsely accuses us of doing.

title: The Son is not stronger than the Father
english: After this Celsus says: “To show that I do not judge these things wide of the mark, I will use their own words. For somewhere in the Heavenly Dialogue they say, in roughly these words: ‘If the Son is stronger than God, and the Son of Man is his lord (and who else will be lord over the God who rules?), how is it that many are around the well and no one goes into the well? Why, when you are travelling so long a road, do you lack courage? It escapes your notice; for I have courage and a sword.’ So their purpose is not to worship the God above the heavens. It is to worship the one they have supposed to be the father of this one around whom they have gathered, so that under the cover of a great God they may pay worship to this one alone whom they put forward, the Son of Man, whom they declare to be stronger than and lord over ‘the God who rules.’ Hence their command not to ‘serve two masters’ (Matthew 6:24), so that the faction around this one man alone may be kept intact.”

Here again he has taken these things from some sect, I do not know which, and a most obscure one, and on their account he accuses all Christians. I call it most obscure because not even we, who have often trained ourselves in debate against people from the sects, can make out the opinion from which Celsus has taken these things, if indeed he took them and did not make them up himself, or add some inference of his own.

For we, who say that the world of the senses too belongs to the One who created all things, say plainly that the Son is not stronger than the Father but less than he. And we say this in obedience to him, since he said: “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28). None of us is so out of his wits as to say: “The Son of Man is lord of God.”

We do say that the Saviour rules, above all when we think of him as God the Word, and Wisdom, and Righteousness, and Truth: he rules all things that have been made subject to him, in so far as he is these, but not also the Father and God who rules him. Then, since the Word does not rule over the unwilling, and there are some still wicked, not only men but also angels and all the demons, we say that he does not yet rule these, since they do not yield to him willingly. But in another sense of “rule” he rules even them, as we say that man rules the irrational animals without having brought their ruling faculty under him: so, by taming them, he rules certain lions and broken-in beasts of burden. Yet he does all things so that he may persuade even those who do not now obey him, and so rule them as well.
So, as far as we are concerned, the saying that Celsus reports as though we proclaimed it is false: “Who else will be lord over the God who rules?”

title: Sayings from another sect
english: Then, I think, again throwing everything into confusion, he brings from another sect the saying “How is it that many are around the well and no one goes into the well?”, and “Why, when you are travelling so long a road, do you lack courage? It escapes your notice,” and “For I have courage and a sword.” We who belong to the Church that bears the name of Christ alone say that none of these things is true.

Having said these things first, he seems to be consistent with himself in saying things that have nothing to do with us. For our purpose is not to worship some God of our own supposing, but the Maker of this universe and of anything else whatever that is neither perceived by the senses nor pointed out. As for those who walk “another way” and “other paths” (Homer, Odyssey 9.261), who deny this Maker and have given themselves to a novel fiction, a God in name only, as though he were greater than the Creator, that is their own affair; and so it is for anyone, if there is such a person, who says that the Son is stronger than and lord over “the God who rules.”

We have already given the account that seems right to us on the saying that one must not “serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). There we also showed that no faction around Jesus the Lord can be shown to exist among those who confess that they have risen above every lord and serve as Lord only the Son of God, the Word of God.

title: Our altars and statues are within
english: After this Celsus says that we shun setting up altars and statues and temples, since he supposes that this is the token by which we keep faith with a hidden and secret fellowship. He does not see that our altars are the ruling mind of each righteous person, from which there truly and spiritually rises fragrant “incense”: “prayers” from a pure conscience. That is why John says in the Revelation: “The incense is the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 5:8); and the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2).

Statues, and offerings fit for God, are with us not made by common artisans. They are given clear shape and form in us by the Word of God: they are the virtues, which are likenesses of “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). In him are the patterns of righteousness and self-control and courage and wisdom and piety and the other virtues. In all, then, who in keeping with the divine Word have fashioned in themselves self-control and righteousness and courage and wisdom and piety, and the works of the other virtues, there are statues. With these, we are convinced, it is fitting to honour the original of all statues: “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), the only-begotten God (John 1:18).

Moreover, those who put off “the old self with its deeds and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created it” (Colossians 3:9–10), taking up the state of being “after the image of the Creator,” make within themselves statues of him, such as the God over all wishes.

Among sculptors some achieve their work marvellously, such as Phidias or Polyclitus, or among painters Zeuxis and Apelles; others make statues less well than these, and others again less well than those of the second rank; and, in a word, there is great difference in the making of statues and images. In the same way some make statues of the God over all better than others, and with perfect knowledge, so that there is no comparison between the Olympian Zeus that Phidias made and the one fashioned after the image of God the Creator (Colossians 3:10). But far better than all those in the whole creation, and surpassing them, is the statue in our Saviour, who says: “The Father is in me” (John 14:11).

title: Living statues where God dwells
english: In each of those who, as far as they are able, have imitated him in this too, there is the statue “after the image of the Creator,” which they make by gazing on God with a pure heart (Matthew 5:8), having become “imitators of God” (Ephesians 5:1). In short, all Christians try to set up altars such as we have described and statues such as we have shown. These are not lifeless and senseless, nor fit to receive the greedy demons who lie in wait by lifeless things. They are fit to receive the Spirit of God, who comes to dwell in the statues of virtue we have spoken of, and in what is “after the image of the Creator,” as in his own home. So too the Spirit of Christ settles upon those who are, if I may call them so, of one form with him.

It was because the word of God wished to set forth such things that it recorded God making this promise to the righteous: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (2 Corinthians 6:16); and the Saviour saying: “If anyone hears my words and does them, I and my Father will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23).

Let anyone who wishes, then, compare the altars I have described with the altars Celsus speaks of, and the statues in the soul of those who are devout toward the God of the universe with the statues of Phidias and Polyclitus and their like. He will see clearly that those are lifeless and decay with time, but these remain in the immortal soul for as long as the rational soul wishes them to remain in it.

title: Our bodies are God’s temple
english: If temples too must be set beside temples, so that we may show those who accept Celsus’s views that we do not shun setting up temples fit for the statues and altars we have described, but that we turn away from building lifeless and dead temples to the Giver of all life, let anyone who wishes hear how we are taught that our bodies are “a temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 6:19), and that “if anyone,” through licentiousness or sin, “destroys the temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3:17), he, as one truly impious toward the true temple, will be destroyed.

But the temple better and more excellent than all those so named was the holy and pure body of our Saviour Jesus. He knew that the temple of the God within him could be plotted against by the impious, yet not in such a way that the purpose of the plotters would be stronger than the Godhead that built the temple. So he says to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). And this “he was saying about the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

In another way, too, the divine Scriptures teach in a hidden sense what concerns the resurrection to those who can hear the words of God with a more divine hearing. They say that the temple will be built again with living and most precious stones, hinting that each of those who are of one spirit, through the same Word, in the piety that accords with him is a precious stone of the whole temple of God. So Peter says: “You are being built up, living stones and a spiritual house, for a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5); and Paul: “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus our Lord himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20).

The passage in Isaiah, too, has some such hidden meaning. It reads as follows, addressed to Jerusalem: “Behold, I am preparing for you carbuncle as your stone, and sapphire as your foundations; and I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates of crystal stones, and your outer wall of choice stones; and all your sons taught by God, and your children in great peace; and in righteousness you shall be built” (Isaiah 54:11–14).

title: Why we shun altars, statues and temples
english: Some of the righteous, then, are carbuncle stone, others sapphire, others jasper, others crystal (Isaiah 54:11–12); and so the righteous are every kind of choice and precious stone. The meaning to be found in these stones, the account of their nature, and the kinds of souls to which the name of each precious stone can be applied, this is not the occasion to set out. It was necessary only to recall briefly the intent of our temples, and of the one temple of God made of precious stones.

For suppose that people in their several cities were taking pride, one against another, in what they count as temples. Those who were proud of their more costly temples would speak of the special excellences of their own in order to show up the inferior ones. In the same way, to those who accuse us because we do not think the divine should be worshipped in senseless temples, we set our own temples against theirs. And we show, at least to those who are not senseless and not like their senseless gods, that there is no comparison between our statues and the statues of the Gentiles; nor between our altars, with what I may call the incense rising from them, and their altars with the smoke of burnt fat and the blood; nor yet between the temples we have described and the temples of senseless gods, admired by senseless men who have not so much as formed a notion of the divine sense (Proverbs 2:5) by which one perceives God and his statues and temples and altars, those that are fitting for God.

It is not, then, to keep faith with a hidden and secret fellowship, nor as any token of that kind, that we shun setting up altars and statues and temples. Rather, because through the teaching of Jesus we have found the manner of piety toward the divine, we shun the things that, under a show of piety, make impious those who have strayed from the piety that comes through Jesus Christ. He alone is the “way” of piety, and he says truly: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

title: Why we do not join the public festivals
english: Let us look also at what Celsus says next about God, and at how he urges us to make use of what are in truth things sacrificed to idols, or, if I may so call them, things sacrificed to demons, though he himself, since he does not know what is truly sacred or what kind of sacrifices are offered to God, would call them “sacred offerings.” What he says is this: “God at any rate is common to all, good, in need of nothing, and free from envy. What then prevents those who are most devoted to Him from taking part in the public festivals as well?”

I do not know what notion led him to think that it follows from God’s being good, in need of nothing, and free from envy, that those devoted to Him should take part in the public festivals. And I say that it would indeed follow from God’s being good, in need of nothing, and free from envy, that they should take part in the public festivals themselves, if it were proved that the public festivals have nothing amiss in them and were instituted from the contemplation of God as fitting for His service and for piety toward Him. If, however, the public festivals, which are festivals in name only, have no reasoned proof that they suit the service of the divine, but are shown to be fictions of men who instituted them haphazardly on account of certain human stories, or fictions that seem to contain natural lore about water or earth or the fruits the earth bears, then plainly those who wish to worship the divine with careful judgment would be acting reasonably in not taking part in the public festivals.

For “a festival,” as one of the Greek wise men well says, “is nothing other than doing what one ought” (Thucydides 1.70). And he truly keeps festival who does “what he ought,” praying always (1 Thessalonians 5:17), and continually offering the bloodless sacrifices in his prayers to the divine. That is why Paul’s words seem to me most lofty: “Do you observe days and months and seasons and years? I fear for you, that I may somehow have labored over you in vain” (Galatians 4:10–11).

title: The perfect man keeps every feast at all times
english: If anyone objects to this by pointing to our own customs on set days, the Lord’s days, the days of Preparation, the Passover, or Pentecost, we must answer this too: the perfect man, who is always in the words, the works, and the thoughts of the Word of God, the One who is Lord by nature, is always in His days and always keeps the Lord’s days. Moreover, since he is always preparing himself for true life, abstaining from the pleasures of life that deceive the many, not feeding “the mind of the flesh” (Romans 8:6), but beating his “body” and bringing it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9:27), he always keeps the days of Preparation.

Further, he who has understood that “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and that we must keep the feast (1 Corinthians 5:8) by eating of the flesh of the Word (John 6:53), never fails to keep the Passover, which means the crossing-over. For he is always crossing over, in his reasoning and in every word and every action, from the affairs of this life to God, and hastening toward His city.

Besides this, he who can say with truth, “We have risen with Christ” (Colossians 3:1), and also, “He raised us up with Him and seated us with Him in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 2:6), is always in the days of Pentecost. This is above all so when, like the apostles of Jesus, he has gone up “into the upper room” (Acts 1:13) and gives himself to supplication and “prayer” (Acts 1:14), so as to become worthy of “the rushing of a mighty wind” from heaven (Acts 2:2), a wind that uses its might to wipe out the wickedness among men and all that comes from it, and worthy also of some share in a tongue of fire from God (Acts 2:3).

title: Set days for the many, an unending feast for the spiritual
english: But the great number of those who are thought to believe, and who are not of such stature, are unwilling or unable to keep all days in this way, and so they need outward examples, perceived by the senses, to remind them, so that they do not drift away altogether (Hebrews 2:1). I think that Paul had this in mind when he called the festival kept on days set apart from the others a “part of a feast” (Colossians 2:16), and that by speaking in this way he hinted that the life lived at all times according to the divine Word is not “in part of a feast,” but in a feast that is complete and unceasing.

Consider then again, from what has been said about our festivals when they are set beside the public festivals of Celsus and of the nations, whether these festivals of ours are not far more worthy of reverence than the public ones, in which “the mind of the flesh” (Romans 8:6) keeps festival and runs riot, turning aside into drunkenness and licentiousness. It would take too long now to explain why the festivals according to the law of God teach us to eat “the bread of affliction” (Deuteronomy 16:3) or “unleavened bread with bitter herbs” (Exodus 12:8), or why they say, “Humble your souls” (Leviticus 16:29), or anything like these.

For it is not possible for man, who is composite, to keep festival with his whole being so long as “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). Either a man keeps festival in the spirit and afflicts the body, which because of “the mind of the flesh” (Romans 8:6) is not of a nature to keep festival together with the spirit; or he keeps festival according to the flesh, and has no room for the festival according to the spirit. But this is enough on the subject of festivals for the present.

title: The table of the Lord and the table of demons
english: Let us see what arguments Celsus uses when he urges us to eat things sacrificed to idols and to share in the public sacrifices at the public festivals. What he says is this: “If these idols are nothing, what is so terrible about taking part in the common feast? But if there are certain demons, clearly these too belong to God, and we must trust them, and offer acceptable sacrifices to them according to the laws, and pray to them, so that they may be well disposed.”

To answer this it is useful to take in hand and make plain the whole discussion of “things sacrificed to idols” (1 Corinthians 8:1) that Paul gives in the First Epistle to the Corinthians. There, meeting the claim that “an idol is nothing in the world” (1 Corinthians 8:4), he established the harm that comes from eating things sacrificed to idols. He shows those who are able to understand what is said there that the one who partakes of things sacrificed to idols is doing nothing short of what a murderer does, since he destroys his own brothers, for whom “Christ died” (1 Corinthians 8:11). And after this, laying it down that what is sacrificed is sacrificed to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20), he shows that those who partake of “the table of demons” become “partners with demons” (1 Corinthians 10:20–21); and he shows that it is impossible for the same man to “partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21).

But since an exposition of what the Epistle to the Corinthians says on these matters requires a whole treatise, argued at greater length, we will be content with what has been briefly given. From it, anyone who examines it will see that even if the idols are nothing, it is none the less a terrible thing, even so, to take part in the common feast of the idols. We have also said enough on the point that even if there are certain demons to whom the sacrifices are offered, we ought not to partake of the offerings, since we know the difference between “the table of the Lord” and “the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21). And because we know it, we do everything so that we may always partake of “the table of the Lord,” and guard ourselves in every way so that we may never become partners at the “table” of “demons.”

title: Demons do not belong to God
english: Since Celsus says in these words that the demons too belong to God, and that for this reason we must trust them, and offer acceptable sacrifices to them according to the laws, and pray to them, so that they may be well disposed, we must teach those who are willing about this point too: the word of God is unwilling to call anything wicked God’s possession, since it judges such a thing unworthy of so great a Lord. That is why not all men are called men of God, but only those who are worthy of God, such as Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1) and Elijah (1 Kings 17:24), and anyone else who is recorded as “a man of God,” or who is like those so recorded.

So too not all angels are said to be “angels of God,” but only the blessed ones; while those who turned aside to wickedness are named angels of the devil (Matthew 25:41), just as wicked men are called men of sin (2 Thessalonians 2:3), or sons of pestilence (1 Samuel 2:12), or sons of unrighteousness. Among men, then, some are good and some are wicked, and for this reason some are said to be “of God” and others of the devil (1 John 3:10); and among “angels” too, some are “of God” and others of the evil one. But demons are not divided in two in this way, for all of them are shown to be wicked.

For this reason we will say that Celsus’s argument is false when he says: “But if there are certain demons, clearly these too belong to God.” Or else let anyone who wishes show either that the division made concerning men and angels is not sound, or that an account like it can be demonstrated in the case of demons as well. But if this cannot be done, it is plain that the demons do not belong to God; for their ruler is not God, but, as the divine words say, “Beelzebul” (Matthew 12:24).

title: We pray only to God, through His Word
english: Nor must we put our trust in demons, even if Celsus urges us toward them. Instead, we must die rather than obey demons, and endure anything whatever in obeying God. In the same way we must not offer acceptable sacrifices to demons, for it is impossible to offer acceptable sacrifices to beings that are wicked and do harm to men.

And according to what laws does Celsus want us to offer acceptable sacrifices to the demons? If according to the laws established in the cities, let him prove that they agree with the divine laws. But if he cannot do this (for the laws of the many cities do not even agree with one another), then clearly they are either not laws in the proper sense, or laws of wicked men, which we must not trust; for “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Away, then, with the counsel of Celsus, who says that we must pray to demons; we must not listen to it even in the least. For we must pray to the God over all, and to Him alone; and indeed we must pray also to the only-begotten Word of God, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). And we must ask Him, as High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), to carry up our prayer, once it has reached Him, to His God and our God, and to His Father and the Father of those who live according to the Word of God (John 20:17).

Just as we would not wish to have men well disposed toward us who want us to live according to their own wickedness, if they are well disposed to none of those who choose the opposite course, since their goodwill makes us enemies of God, who perhaps does not become well disposed to those who wish to have such men well disposed toward them; in the same way, those who have understood the nature of demons, their will, and their wickedness would never wish to have the demons well disposed.

title: Guarded by God, we fear no demon
english: For even if the demons are not well disposed toward them, they could suffer nothing from them, since they are guarded by the God over all, who is well disposed toward them because of their piety, and who sets His divine angels over those worthy of being guarded, so that they suffer nothing from the demons. He who has the God over all well disposed toward him through his piety toward Him, and through having received the Lord Jesus, God’s Angel “of Great Counsel” (Isaiah 9:6), and who is content with the goodwill of God through Christ Jesus, could say with confidence, as one who will suffer nothing from the whole army of demons: “The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Psalm 27:1). And he will also say: “If an army is drawn up against me, my heart will not fear” (Psalm 27:3).

So much, then, in answer to the words: “But if there are certain demons, clearly these too belong to God, and we must trust them, and offer acceptable sacrifices to them according to the laws, and pray to them, so that they may be well disposed.”

title: Celsus on abstaining from sacrificial meat
english: Let us set out the next passage as well, and once again examine it as best we can. It runs as follows: “If, by some ancestral custom, they abstain from certain sacrificial victims of this kind, then they must surely abstain from eating any animal at all, as Pythagoras too thinks, who honours the soul and its instruments. But if, as they say, it is so that they may not feast with demons, I congratulate them on their wisdom, that they are slow to see that they are always the table-companions of demons. They guard against this only when they see a victim being sacrificed. But when they eat bread and drink wine and taste fruits, and drink even water itself and breathe the very air, do they not receive each of these from certain demons, to each of whom the care of his own share has been assigned?”

I do not know how he came to think it follows from this that those whom he described as abstaining from certain victims by some ancestral custom must abstain from eating any animal at all. And we do not say this as though the divine word did not also counsel such things, and did not say, for the sake of a safer and purer life: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything by which your brother stumbles” (Romans 14:21); and again: “Do not by your food destroy the one for whom Christ died” (Romans 14:15); and again: “If meat makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not make my brother stumble” (1 Corinthians 8:13).

title: Jesus and the apostles on foods
english: It should be understood, however, that while the Jews think they understand the law of Moses, and in the matter of foods keep the rule of eating what they hold to be clean and abstaining from what is unclean, and also of not using an animal’s blood for food, nor what has been torn by wild beasts, and other such things (there is much to say about these, and for that reason this is not the right time to examine them), the teaching of Jesus wished to call all men to the pure worship of God, and not, on the pretext of a heavier law about foods, to hinder many of those whose character could be helped by Christianity. So it declared: “It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth” (Matthew 15:11). For what “goes into the mouth,” he says, “passes into the stomach and is cast out into the drain” (Matthew 15:17); but what comes out of the mouth are “evil thoughts” put into words, and “murders,” “adulteries,” “fornications,” “thefts,” “false witness,” and “blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19).

Paul too says: “Food will not commend us to God; for if we eat, we are no better off, and if we do not eat, we are no worse off” (1 Corinthians 8:8). Then, since these words have a certain obscurity unless they are spelled out, “it seemed good to the apostles” of Jesus “and to the elders” who had gathered together at Antioch, and, as they themselves put it, “to the Holy Spirit,” to write a letter to the believers from among the Gentiles (Acts 15:22–23, 28). The only foods this letter forbade them to eat were those which, as they put it, were “necessary”: that is, things offered to idols, or things strangled, or blood (Acts 15:28–29).

title: Why Christians abstain from certain foods
english: For what is offered to idols is sacrificed to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20), and the man of God must not become a partaker in “the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21). As for things strangled, from which the blood has not been drained (and blood, they say, is the food of demons, who feed on the vapours that rise from it), the word forbids them, so that we may not be fed with the food of demons; for perhaps some such spirits would be fed along with us if we ate things strangled. And from what has been said about “things strangled,” the reason for abstaining from “blood” can be made clear.

Now that I have come to these matters, it is not out of place for me to recall a most elegant saying, recorded in the Sentences of Sextus, which most Christians also read. It runs as follows: “The use of living creatures is a matter of indifference, but abstaining from them is more in keeping with reason” (Sentences of Sextus 109). So we do not abstain merely by some ancestral custom from what are held to be sacrificial victims and are offered to the so-called gods or heroes or demons, but for several reasons, some of which I have set out in part.

Nor is it the case that, just as one must abstain from all wickedness and from what comes of wickedness, so one must abstain from eating any animal at all. Rather, one must abstain not only from eating animals but from anything whatever, if our use of food should spring from wickedness and from what comes of wickedness. For one must abstain from eating out of gluttony, or because one is led by pleasure, without the aim of the body’s health and its care.

Since we in no way say that there is a transmigration of the soul and a fall of it as far down as the irrational animals, it is clear that, if we sometimes abstain from animals, it is not in the manner of Pythagoras that we refrain from using their flesh. For we know how to honour only the rational soul, and to commit its instruments with honour to burial according to custom. For it is right that the dwelling place of the rational soul should not be cast aside without honour, carelessly, like that of the irrational creatures; and above all because Christians have believed that honour reaches even to the body in which a rational soul has dwelt, since it received a soul that contended well through such an instrument. As for “How are the dead raised, and with what kind of body do they come?” (1 Corinthians 15:35), we have shown this above in a few words, as this treatise required.

title: Unseen stewards and demon executioners
english: After this, Celsus sets down what Christians and Jews alike say when they defend their abstaining from things offered to idols and declare that those who are devoted to the God over all must not feast with demons. It was in answer to this that he said what has been quoted. So far as foods and drinks are concerned, we know no other ways of feasting with demons than these: when someone eats what most people call sacred offerings, and drinks the wine of the libations poured to demons. But Celsus thinks that even the man who eats bread, and drinks wine in any way at all, and tastes fruits, feasts with demons. Indeed, even if someone takes only water, he says that in this too the drinker feasts with demons. And to this he adds that the man who breathes this air also receives it from certain demons, since the demons set over the air grant living creatures the air they breathe.

Let anyone who wishes, then, take the side of Celsus’s argument, and show how it is not certain divine angels of God, but demons, whose whole race is evil, who have been appointed to manage all the things just mentioned. For we too say that it is not without the oversight of invisible farmers, if I may call them so, and of other stewards, not only of what grows from the earth but also of all flowing water and of the air, that the earth brings forth what is said to be governed by nature, that water pours forth and runs in springs and in rivers that rise of themselves, and that the air is kept uncorrupted and becomes life-giving to those who breathe it.

Yet we do not say that these invisible beings are demons. But if one must venture to say something, and if these things really are the work of demons, we shall say this: famines, failures of the vine and of fruit trees, droughts, and also the corruption of the air to the ruin of crops, and sometimes even to the death of animals and to plague among men, all these the demons bring about with their own hands, as executioners. They have received authority by a certain divine judgment to work these things at certain times, either for the conversion of men who have been carried away into the flood of wickedness, or else for the training of the rational race.

This happens so that those who remain pious even amid such great calamities, and in no way become worse, may become manifest to the spectators, invisible and visible, who until then did not see their true state; while those who are disposed the opposite way but hide the display of their wickedness, being shown up by events for what they are, may become aware of themselves and may become plain to the spectators, if I may call them so.

title: We feast with angels, not demons
english: The psalmist bears witness that by divine judgment the grimmer things are carried out by certain evil angels, when he says: “He sent upon them the wrath of his anger, anger and wrath and affliction, a mission by evil angels” (Psalm 78:49). If anything else besides these also happens when the demons are given leave, since they always wish to do such things but cannot always do them because they are restrained, let whoever is able examine it, picturing the divine judgment, so far as human nature can, concerning the release of many souls from the body all at once, by such roads as lead to that death which is neither good nor evil.

For “great are the judgments of God,” and because of their greatness they cannot be grasped by a mind still bound to a mortal body; that is why they are also “hard to describe” (Wisdom of Solomon 17:1), and to uninstructed souls they cannot be seen in even the smallest measure. That is also why the more rash, through their ignorance of these matters and the scrutiny their rashness turns upon the divine, add to the impious doctrines against providence.

We do not, then, receive from demons each of the things that serve the needs of life, especially those of us who have learned to use them as we ought. Nor do those who partake of bread and wine and fruits and water and air feast with demons, but rather with divine angels appointed over such things. These angels are, as it were, invited to the table of the pious man who has heard the word that teaches such things as this: “Whether you eat or drink or do anything, do all things to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). And again in another place it is written: “Whether you eat or drink,” do all things “in the name” of God (Colossians 3:17; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

So when we eat and drink and breathe “to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31), and do all things according to the word, we feast with none of the demons, but with the divine angels. For “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Timothy 4:4–5). But it would not be “good,” nor could it be sanctified, if, as Celsus thinks, these things had been assigned to demons.

title: Thanks to the Creator, not to demons
english: From this it is clear that we have also answered what he says next, which runs as follows: “Either, then, one must not live at all, anywhere, nor come into this world; or one who has come into life on these terms must give thanks to the demons who have been allotted the things on earth, and render them first-fruits and prayers as long as we live, so that we may find them kind to men.”

We must indeed live, and we must live according to the word of God, so far as is possible and so far as it is granted to live according to it. And it is granted when, whether we eat or drink, we do “all things to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). We must not refuse to use, with thanksgiving to the Creator, the works he has made for our sake. It is on these terms, rather than those Celsus thinks, that we have been brought into life by God; and we are not subject to demons, but to the God over all, through Jesus Christ, who has brought us to him (1 Peter 3:18).

By the laws of God no demon has been allotted the things on earth. But because of their own lawlessness, perhaps they have shared out among themselves the places where the knowledge of God and of the life that accords with him is wholly lacking, or where those estranged from the divine are many. Or perhaps, as fit to be overseers and punishers of the wicked, they were appointed by the Word who governs the universe to rule over those who have made themselves subject to wickedness and not to God.

For such reasons, then, let Celsus, as one who does not know God, render his thank-offerings to demons. But we, giving thanks to the Maker of the universe, also eat the loaves that are offered with thanksgiving and prayer over the gifts. Through the prayer these loaves become a body, something holy, which sanctifies those who use it with a sound purpose.

title: Our first-fruits go to the Creator
english: Celsus would have first-fruits, too, dedicated to demons. But we dedicate them to the One who said, “Let the earth bring forth the green plant, sowing seed according to its kind and likeness, and the fruit tree bearing fruit whose seed is in it according to its kind upon the earth” (Genesis 1:11). And to the One to whom we render our first-fruits we also send up our prayers, “having a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Hebrews 4:14), and we hold fast “the confession” (Hebrews 4:14) as long as we live, finding God and his Only-begotten, who is made manifest to us in Jesus, kind toward us.

And if we long also for a multitude of beings whose kindness we wish to win, we learn “that a thousand thousands stood beside him, and ten thousand times ten thousand ministered to him” (Daniel 7:10). These, seeing as their kindred and friends those who imitate their own piety toward God, work together for the salvation of those who call upon God and pray sincerely. They appear to them, and they think they must listen to them and, as if at a single signal, come among them to benefit and save those who pray to God, to whom they themselves also pray. For “they are all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14).

Let the wise men of the Greeks, then, say that demons have been allotted the human soul from its birth. But Jesus taught us not to despise even “the little ones” in the Church, saying that “their angels always behold the face of my Father in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), and the prophet says, “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Psalm 34:7).

So we too do not deny that there are many demons on earth. We say that they exist and have power among the wicked because of the wickedness of such people, but that they have no power against those who have put on “the whole armour of God” (Ephesians 6:11) and have taken up strength “to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11, 13), and who are always studying their wrestling holds, because they know “that our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12).

title: Would God’s officers take revenge?
english: Let us consider another passage of Celsus too, which runs thus: “Or could the satrap, governor, general or procurator of the king of the Persians or of the Romans, and even those who hold lesser offices, charges or services, do great harm if neglected, while the satraps and ministers of the air and of the earth would do little harm if insulted?”

See how he brings in satraps of the God over all, modelled on human ones, with governors, generals and procurators, and those who hold lesser offices, charges and services, doing great harm to those who insult them. He does not see that not even a wise man would wish to harm anyone, but would rather, as far as he could, turn even those who insult him and make them better. Unless, perhaps, the satraps, governors and generals of the God over all, as Celsus pictures them, are worse than Lycurgus, the lawgiver of the Spartans, and Zeno of Citium. For Lycurgus, when he was given power over the man who had knocked out his eye, not only took no revenge on him but never stopped working on him with persuasive words until he had won him over to philosophy. And Zeno, when someone said to him, “May I perish if I do not punish you,” replied, “And I, if I do not make you my friend.”

And I do not yet speak of those whose character has been formed by the teaching of Jesus and who have heard the words, “Love your enemies and pray for those who mistreat you, so that you may become sons of your Father in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the wicked and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous” (Matthew 5:44–45). And in the prophetic writings the righteous man says such things as these: “O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is unrighteousness in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then may I fall back empty-handed from my enemies; then may the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground” (Psalm 7:3–5).

title: Demons cannot harm those devoted to God
english: But the true satraps, governors, generals and procurators of God, the angels, do not harm those who insult them, as Celsus thinks. And if some demons, of the kind Celsus too has pictured, do harm, they harm as wicked beings who have been entrusted by God with no satrapy, command or stewardship; and they harm those who are subject to them and have submitted to them as masters.

Perhaps it is for this reason too that people in each place who break the law about foods that custom says must not be eaten are harmed, if they are among those under those demons. But if some are not under them and have not submitted themselves to the demon of the place, they are free from suffering at their hands, having bidden a long farewell to such demons; yet if, through ignorance about other things, they have submitted themselves to other demons, they can suffer at the hands of those.

But a Christian, a true Christian, who has submitted himself to God alone and to his Word, would suffer nothing from demons, since he is stronger than demons. And he would certainly suffer nothing, since “the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Psalm 34:7), and his angel, who “always” beholds “the face of the Father in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), ever carries up his prayers through the only High Priest to the God of the universe, and himself prays together with the one entrusted to his care.

So let Celsus not frighten us with bogeys, threatening us with harm from the demons if we neglect them. For demons, if neglected, could do nothing to us who are devoted to the One who alone is able to help all who are worthy, and who no less sets his own angels over those who are devout toward him, so that neither the opposing angels nor the one who is called their “ruler of this age” (compare 1 Corinthians 2:6; John 12:31) can do anything against those who are devoted to God.

title: God hears prayer in every language
english: Then, forgetting that he is talking to Christians, who pray to God alone through Jesus, and mixing up what belongs to others and attaching it to Christians without reason, he says: “If one names them in a barbarian tongue they will have power, but if in Greek or Latin, no longer.”

Let him show, then, whom we name in a barbarian tongue as though calling on him for help. And let anyone who observes the following be persuaded that Celsus said these things against us to no purpose: that Christians in general do not even use, in their prayers, the names that are set down in the divine Scriptures and applied to God. Rather, the Greeks use Greek names and the Romans Latin ones, and so each prays to God in his own language and sings his praise as best he can. And the Lord of every language hears those who pray in every language as though he heard, if I may put it so, a single voice, the voice of what they mean, made plain through the varied languages. For the God over all is not one of those who have been allotted some language, barbarian or Greek, and who know none of the others, or do not know how to attend to those who speak in other languages.

title: Christians do not revile the statues
english: Then after this, having heard either no Christian at all or some lawless and uneducated one from among the many, he says that Christians say: “Look, I stand beside the statue of Zeus or Apollo or any god you please, and I revile it and strike it, and it does nothing to avenge itself on me.”

He does not see that in the divine law it is also commanded, “You shall not revile gods” (Exodus 22:28), so that our mouths may not grow used to reviling anyone at all; for we hear, “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12:14), and we are taught that “revilers” will not “inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10). Who among us is so foolish as to say such things, and not see that a thing of this kind does nothing to overthrow the belief in the reputed gods? For even those who are wholly godless, who have done away with providence and by their wicked and impious doctrines have founded a school of so-called philosophers, have not themselves suffered any of the things that the many regard as evils, nor have those who embraced their doctrines; on the contrary, they are rich and healthy in body.

But if anyone looks for harm in them, let him see that they are the ones truly harmed. For what greater harm is there than not to perceive the Maker from the order of the world? And what misery is worse than to have one’s mind blinded and not to see the Creator and Father of every mind?

title: Jesus is no demon
english: Having put such words in our mouths and slandered Christians, who say no such things, he thinks he is furnishing himself with a defence, though it is a jest rather than a defence. In it he says, as if to us: “Do you not see, my good man, that someone takes his stand and not only blasphemes even your demon, but has him banished by proclamation from every land and sea, and binds you, who are consecrated to him like a statue, leads you away and impales you; and the demon, or, as you say, the Son of God, takes no vengeance on him?”

This defence would have had some place if we used such words as he has written down that we say; and yet even then he would not have spoken the truth in calling the Son of God a demon. In our view, since we say that all demons are wicked, the One who turned so many people to God is not a demon but God the Word and Son of God. But according to Celsus, who has made nothing plain about wicked demons and has forgotten himself, how I do not know, Jesus is called a demon.
Later, however, after all the remedies that they did not accept, what is said about the ungodly will come upon those who are found in what one might call incurable wickedness.

title: The mills of the gods and the justice of God
english: We, for our part, whatever we may say about punishment, do turn many from their sins through the teaching about punishment. But let us consider what sort of answer the priest of Apollo or of Zeus gives in Celsus’s account: “Late,” he says, “grind the mills of the gods, even to children’s children, who may be born later.”

See how much better than this are the words, “Fathers shall not die for children, nor shall sons die for fathers; each shall die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16), and this, “The one who ate the sour grape shall have his teeth set on edge” (Jeremiah 31:30), and this, “A son shall not bear the unrighteousness of his father, and a father shall not bear the unrighteousness of his son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the lawlessness of the lawless shall be upon him” (Ezekiel 18:20).

But if anyone says that the words, “repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me” (Deuteronomy 5:9; compare Exodus 20:5), are like “to children’s children, who may be born later,” let him learn that in Ezekiel such a saying is called a “parable” (Ezekiel 18:2–3), where the prophet blames those who say, “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Ezekiel 18:2; compare Jeremiah 31:29), and to this is added, “As I live, says the Lord” (Ezekiel 18:3), “but each shall die for his own sin” (Jeremiah 31:30). This is not the right time to explain what the parable means about “sins” being repaid “to the third and fourth generation.”

title: We revile neither statues nor demons
english: Next, railing at us like old women, he says: “You revile their statues and laugh at them. But if you had reviled Dionysus himself or Heracles while he was present, perhaps you would not have got away with it. Yet those who stretched out and punished your God when he was present suffered nothing for doing it, nor even afterwards, in all the long life that followed. What new thing has happened since then to make anyone believe that he was not a human sorcerer but a child of God? And the one who sent his son for the sake of certain messages, it seems, looked on while he was punished so cruelly that the messages were destroyed with him, and in all the time that has passed since then he has paid no heed. What father is so unholy? Now perhaps he wished it, as you say, and that is why he suffered outrage. But as for these whom you blaspheme, one could have said that they too wish it, and for that reason bear being blasphemed; for it is best to compare like with like. But these at least take vigorous vengeance on the one who blasphemes them, so that he either flees for this reason and hides, or is caught and perishes.”

To this I would answer that we revile no one, for we are persuaded that “revilers” will not “inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10), and we read, “Bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28), and, “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12:14). We know also the saying, “When reviled, we bless” (1 Corinthians 4:12). And if reviling has some justification as self-defence for one who thinks he has been wronged, yet the word of God does not allow us even this, how much more must we refrain from reviling where reviling shows great folly? It is equally foolish to revile stone or gold or silver, shaped into the form of gods that is customary among those who are far from the divine. So we do not laugh at the lifeless images either, but, if at anyone, at those who worship them.

Nor, even if there are demons settled in certain statues, and one of them is thought to be Dionysus and another Heracles, do we revile them either. Such a thing is futile, and in no way fits the man who is gentle, peaceable and calm of soul, and who has learned that one must not revile anyone, man or demon, even for his wickedness.

title: The city that crucified Jesus
english: I do not know how Celsus has fallen, without meaning to, into showing by the facts that those whom a little earlier he praised as demons or gods are thoroughly base, taking revenge to repay an injury rather than punishing to correct, whenever someone reviles them. For he says: “If you had reviled Dionysus himself or Heracles while he was present, perhaps you would not have got away with it.” Let anyone who wishes explain how one who is not present hears anything, and why he is sometimes present and sometimes not, and what business demons have in moving from place to place.

After this he goes on, supposing that we call God the body of Jesus that was stretched out and punished, and not the divinity in him, and that it was held to be God at the time it was stretched out and punished: “But those who stretched out and punished your God when he was present suffered nothing for doing it.” We have said a good deal earlier about the human sufferings he underwent, and now we pass over the subject on purpose, so as not to seem to repeat ourselves.

But since he says that those who punished Jesus suffered nothing even afterwards, in all the long life that followed, we will show him, and all who wish to learn, what became of the city in which the Jewish people demanded that Jesus be crucified, saying, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23:21). For they preferred that the robber, who had been thrown “into prison for insurrection and murder,” be released, “but Jesus” (Luke 23:19; Luke 23:25), who had been handed over “out of envy” (Matthew 27:18; Mark 15:10), be crucified. Not long afterwards that city was attacked in war and besieged for so long a time that it was overturned from its foundations and laid waste. For God judged those who lived in that place unworthy of the life that people share in common. Indeed, if I may say something strange, it was in sparing them, and seeing that they were past cure and could not be changed for the better, and were growing every day in the flood of their wickedness, that he handed them over to their enemies. And these things happened because of the blood of Jesus, poured out through their plot upon their land, which could no longer bear those who had dared so great a sacrilege against Jesus.

title: A holy Father and a grain of wheat
english: So something new has indeed happened since the time when Jesus suffered: I mean what befell the city and the whole nation, and the sudden birth of a nation of Christians, born, as it were, all at once (Isaiah 66:8). New too is this, that those who were strangers to “the covenants” of God and aliens from the promises (Ephesians 2:12), those far from the truth, have received it by a certain divine power. These were not the doings of a human sorcerer but the works of God. He sent, for the sake of his messages, his own Word in Jesus, who was punished so cruelly that the cruelty is charged against those who punished him unjustly, and who bore it with the greatest courage and with all gentleness.

His punishment did not destroy God’s messages but, if it must be put this way, made them known; as Jesus himself taught when he said, “Unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). So by dying, Jesus, “the grain of wheat,” bore “much fruit,” and the Father always takes care of the fruits that have come, still come, and will yet come from the death of the grain “of wheat.” A holy father, then, is the Father of Jesus, who did not spare “his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), him who was his own lamb, so that “the Lamb of God,” who dies for the whole world, might take away “the sin of the world” (John 1:29). And for the world’s sake he endured, not under compulsion but willingly, the things the insolent inflicted on him.

Then, after this, Celsus takes up again his argument against those who blaspheme the statues, and says: “But as for these whom you blaspheme, one could have said that they too wish it, and for that reason bear being blasphemed; for it is best to compare like with like.
