But these at least take vigorous vengeance on the one who blasphemes them, so that he either flees for this reason and hides, or is caught and perishes.” It is not, then, as blasphemers that the demons think they take vengeance on Christians, but as those who drive them out of the images and out of human bodies and souls. For without understanding what happens, Celsus has said something true on this point. It is true that the souls of those who condemn Christians, of those who betray them, and of those who delight in making war on Christians, are filled with wicked demons.

title: Martyrs break the power of demons
english: But the souls of those who die for Christianity out of piety, leaving the body with glory, were pulling down the power of the demons and weakening their plots against mankind. That, I think, is why the demons, having learned by experience that they were being defeated and overcome by the martyrs of the truth, were afraid to return to taking vengeance. And so, until they forget the pains they have suffered, the world is likely to be at peace with Christians. But when they gather their strength, and, blinded by wickedness, wish again to take vengeance and to persecute Christians, they will be pulled down again; and then once more the souls of the godly, who for piety’s sake put off their bodies, will pull down the army of the evil one.

For my part I think that the demons, perceiving that those who conquer and die for piety pull down their dominion, while those who are overcome by the pains and deny their reverence for God become subject to them, sometimes strive hard against the Christians who are handed over, as though they were tormented by their confession and relieved by their denial. Traces of this may be seen in the judges too, who are tormented by those who endure the outrages and the tortures, but exult whenever a Christian is defeated. Nor is it out of the kindness they seem to have that they do this, since they see plainly that the “tongue” of those overcome by pain “has sworn, but the mind” is “unsworn” (Euripides, Hippolytus 612).

This too in reply to his words: “But these at least take vigorous vengeance on the one who blasphemes them, so that he either flees for this reason and hides, or is caught and perishes.” Even if a Christian flees, he does not flee from cowardice, but in keeping with the command of his Teacher (Matthew 10:23), and he keeps himself pure for the salvation of others who are yet to be helped.

title: Celsus’s list of oracles and portents
english: Let us look also at what comes next, which runs as follows: “Why need I list all that has been foretold with inspired voice, partly from the oracles by prophets and prophetesses, partly by other men and women who were possessed? All the marvels that have been heard from the inner shrines themselves? All that has been made known to inquirers from victims and sacrifices, and all from other portentous signs? To some, clear visions have appeared. All of life is full of these things. How many cities have been restored by oracles and rid themselves of plagues and famines, and how many, by neglecting or forgetting them, have been miserably destroyed? How many have been sent out to found a colony and, by carrying out what was commanded, have prospered? How many rulers, how many private persons, have fared better or worse because of this? How many, distressed at being childless, gained what they prayed for and escaped the wrath of demons? How many have been healed of bodily maiming? How many again, after committing outrage at the temples, were caught at once, some seized with madness on that very spot, others even confessing what they had done, others taking their own lives, others bound fast by incurable diseases? And before now a dreadful voice from the inner shrines themselves has struck some down.”

I do not know how Celsus brings these things forward as clearly true, while he has held that the wonders recorded among us, whether those of the Jews or those about Jesus and his disciples, are myths. Why should ours not be true, and what Celsus tells be fabricated myths? Not even the philosophical schools of the Greeks have believed his stories, such as the schools of Democritus, Epicurus and Aristotle. Yet perhaps they would have believed ours, because of their clear evidence, if they had met Moses, or one of the prophets who worked marvels, or Jesus himself.

title: Our prophets did all this and more
english: The Pythia is recorded to have once given oracles even after she had been bribed. But our prophets were admired for the clear truth of what they said, not only by the people of their own day but in later times as well. For through the oracles the prophets gave, cities were restored, men were made well, and famines came to an end. Indeed, the whole nation of the Jews plainly went out as a colony from Egypt to Palestine in keeping with oracles; when it carried out what God commanded, it prospered, and when it went astray, it repented. Why need I tell how many rulers and how many private persons, according to the histories of Scripture, fared better or worse by heeding the prophecies or neglecting them?

And if we must speak of childlessness too, and of those who, distressed at it, became fathers or mothers after sending up their prayers about it to the Maker of the universe, let anyone read the story of Abraham and Sarah, from whom Isaac was born when they were already old (Genesis 21:1–7), the father of the whole Jewish nation and of others besides. Let him read also the story of Hezekiah, who not only gained release from his illness in keeping with the prophecies of Isaiah (Isaiah 38:1–8), but also said with confidence: “For from now on I will beget children, who will declare your righteousness” (Isaiah 38:19). And in the second book of Kings, the woman who received Elisha, after he had prophesied by the grace of God that a child would be born, became a mother in answer to Elisha’s prayers (2 Kings 4:8–17).

Besides, countless maimings were healed by Jesus. And others who dared, at the temple in Jerusalem, to outrage the Jewish worship suffered what is recorded in the books of the Maccabees (2 Maccabees 3:24–28).

title: Weighing the wonders by their results
english: But the Greeks will say that these things are myths, even though two whole nations bear witness that they are true. And why are the stories of the Greeks not myths rather than these? Suppose, however, that someone meets the argument head on, and, so as not to seem to accept his own accounts arbitrarily while disbelieving those of others, says that the Greek wonders too were done by certain demons; the Jewish ones either by God through the prophets, or by the angels, or by God through the angels; and the Christian ones by Jesus and by His power at work in the apostles. Come, then, let us set them all side by side and look at the end that those who worked them had in view, and at the benefit or harm, or neither, that came of it to those who received what were thought to be benefits.

Will such a person not see that the Jewish nation of old was a nation of philosophers, before they behaved outrageously toward the Divine, by whom they were forsaken because of their great wickedness; and that the Christians, who came together against all expectation, were drawn at the beginning more by wonders than by words of exhortation to abandon their ancestral ways and to choose ways foreign to those of their fathers? For if we must also use the argument from likelihood about how the Christians first came together, we shall say that it is not credible that the apostles of Jesus, unlettered and ordinary men (Acts 4:13), took courage to proclaim Christianity to men from anything other than the power given to them and the grace in their word for setting forth the things it proclaimed; nor is it credible that those who heard them were moved from long-standing ancestral customs, unless some remarkable power and wondrous deeds had moved them toward teachings so strange and so foreign to those they had been brought up with.

title: Which teachers of punishment change lives
english: Then, I do not know how, Celsus, after bringing forward the zeal of those who contend even to death rather than forswear Christianity, goes on as though putting our teachings on a level with what the initiators and mystagogues say, and he says: “Indeed, my good sir, just as you believe in eternal punishments, so too do the interpreters of those sacred rites, the initiators and mystagogues. You threaten others with them, and they threaten you. For one may well examine which of the two are truer or more powerful. As far as words go, you and they alike affirm your own claims with equal confidence; but if proofs were needed, they display many clear ones, bringing forward the works of certain demonic powers and of oracles, and proofs drawn from divinations of every kind.”

By this, then, he would have it that we and the initiators alike speak of eternal punishments, and he wants to inquire which of the two speak more truly. I would say that those speak the truth who have been able to bring their hearers to live as men convinced that these things are so. Jews and Christians are so convinced about what they call the age to come, and about the rewards in it for the righteous and the punishments for sinners. Let Celsus, then, or anyone who wishes, show who have been brought to such conviction about eternal punishments by the initiators and mystagogues. For it is likely that the aim of anyone who fathers such teachings is not merely to discharge a formality by speaking about punishments, but to bring his hearers, as far as lies in their power, to guard against doing the things that lead to punishment.

Moreover, to those who read them with care, the prophecies seem to me enough, by the foreknowledge they contain, to persuade anyone who reads with understanding and fairness that the Spirit of God was in those men. With these prophecies none of the demonic works that are displayed, none of the powers that come from oracles, and none of the divinations can be compared in the slightest degree.

title: Celsus mocks our hope for the body
english: Let us look also at what Celsus says to us next, which runs as follows: “And further, how is this not absurd of you, to long for the body and to hope that this very body will rise again, as though nothing in us were better or more precious than it, and then again to cast it into punishments as a thing without honour? But with those who are persuaded of this and are wedded to the body it is not worth reasoning about this matter; for these are people who are boorish and unclean in other respects too, and who, without reason, share in the sickness of faction. But those who hope that the soul or the mind (whether they wish to call it spiritual, or an intellectual spirit, holy and blessed, or a living soul (Genesis 2:7), or the incorruptible offspring, from beyond the heavens, of a divine and bodiless nature, or whatever name they like to give it) will be theirs for ever with God, with these I will reason. They are right at least in believing this: that those who have lived well will be happy, while the unjust will be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils. And from this doctrine let neither these nor any other man ever depart.”

As to the resurrection, even if he himself has already reproached us with it many times, we have set forth, as best we could, what seemed reasonable to us on that subject, and we do not intend to make our defence many times over against one charge made many times over. But Celsus slanders us when he says that we think nothing in our make-up better or more precious than the body. For we say that the soul, and above all the rational soul, is a thing more precious than any body, since the soul can receive what is “according to the image of Him who created” it (Colossians 3:10), while the body cannot at all. For in our view God is not a body either, and so we do not fall into the absurdities into which those fall who follow the philosophy of Zeno and Chrysippus.

title: Why we long for the resurrection
english: Since he also reproaches us as men who long for the body, let him know that if longing is a bad thing, we long for nothing; but if it is neither good nor bad, we long for all that God promises to the righteous. In this way, then, we long for and hope for the resurrection of the righteous (Luke 14:14). Celsus thinks, too, that we contradict ourselves when we hope for the resurrection of the body as worthy of honour from God, and yet cast it into punishments as without honour. Now nothing is without honour that suffers for the sake of piety and chooses hardships for the sake of virtue; but everything is without honour that is consumed in pleasures joined with wickedness. So the divine word too says: “What seed is honoured? The seed of man. What seed is without honour? The seed of man” (Sirach 10:19).

Then Celsus thinks that one ought not to reason with those who hope for what concerns the body, since they are irrationally wedded to a thing that cannot attain what they hope for. He calls them boorish and unclean, and says they keep company with faction without reason, when he ought, as a lover of mankind, to help even the more boorish. For the circle of fellowship has not been drawn so as to shut out the more boorish among men, as it shuts out the irrational animals; rather, He who made us made us fit for fellowship with all men alike. It is worthwhile, then, to reason with the boorish too, and to bring them, as far as we can, to greater refinement; and with the unclean, and to make them, as far as possible, cleaner; and with those who, whatever they think, think it without reason and are sick in soul, so that they may no longer do anything without reason nor be sick in soul.

title: Celsus should have defended the doctrine he approves
english: After this he approves of those who hope that the soul, or the mind, or what they call the spiritual or rational spirit, intellectual, holy and blessed, or the living soul (Genesis 2:7), will be theirs for ever and will be with God; and he admits as rightly held both the doctrine that those who have lived well will be happy and the doctrine that the unjust will be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils. And of all that Celsus says, what amazes me most is what he adds to these words, where he says: “And from this doctrine let neither these nor any other man ever depart.”

Writing against Christians, for whom the whole foundation of faith is God, and the promises made through Christ concerning the righteous, and the teachings about punishment concerning the unjust, he ought to have seen this: a Christian overthrown by accepting Celsus’s arguments against Christians would in all likelihood, in throwing away the teaching, throw away with it the very doctrine from which, he says, neither Christians nor any other man should depart.

But Chrysippus, I think, acted more humanely than Celsus in his Therapeutic book On the Passions. Wishing to heal the passions, since they press hard upon the human soul and trouble it, he does so first by the arguments that seemed sound to him, but secondly and thirdly even by doctrines that did not please him. “For even if there are three kinds of goods,” he says, “even so the passions must be healed; one should not, while the passions are inflamed, busy oneself with the doctrine that has already taken hold of the one troubled by passion, so that the cure that is still possible may not be lost through untimely labour over overturning the doctrines that have already seized the soul.” And he says: “Even if pleasure is the good, and the one mastered by passion thinks so, he must none the less be helped and shown that every passion is inconsistent even with the views of those who make pleasure the good and the end.”

Celsus too, then, once he had said that he accepted the doctrines that those who have lived well will be happy and that the unjust will be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils, ought to have acted consistently with himself, and, if he could, after what seemed to him the principal argument, to have built further upon it and to have shown with further arguments that the unjust will truly be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils and that those who have lived well will be happy.

title: Persuading outsiders of the judgment to come
english: For we too, first of all, because of the many, indeed countless, things that have persuaded us to live according to Christianity, wish, as far as we can, to win all men over to the whole of the Christian teaching. But where we find people already prejudiced by slander against Christians, so that, imagining that Christians are not even pious, they will not so much as lend their ears to those who offer to teach them the things of the divine word, there, out of love for mankind, we take our stand as best we can, so that by establishing at least the doctrines about eternal punishment for the ungodly, we may bring even those who are unwilling to become Christians to accept that teaching.

In the same way we wish to instil conviction about those who have lived well too, since we see that even those who are strangers to the faith say many of the same things as we do about a sound way of life. For one would not find anyone who has wholly lost the common notions about what is noble and what is shameful, what is just and what is unjust.

Let all men, then, seeing the world and the ordered motion in it of the heavens and of the fixed stars, and the order of the so-called planets, which move contrary to the motion of the world; seeing also the tempering of the air for the good of living things, and above all of men, and the abundance of things made for the sake of men, beware of doing anything displeasing to the Creator of the universe and of their own souls and of the mind within them. And let them be convinced that they will be punished for their sins, and that they will be led by Him who orders each according to his desert to rewards in proportion to their right actions or to the works they have duly performed. And let all men be convinced that for their better deeds they will fare well, while the wicked will be wretchedly handed over to toils and torments for their injustices, their licentiousness and intemperance, and also for their unmanliness, their cowardice, and all their folly.

title: Celsus should at least have doubted
english: Having said this much on this passage as well, let us look at another statement of Celsus, which runs thus: “Since men are born bound to a body — whether for the sake of the ordering of the universe, or paying the penalty for sin, or because the soul is weighed down by certain passions until it is cleansed in the appointed cycles, for according to Empedocles ‘thrice ten thousand seasons it must wander far from the blessed, becoming in the course of time every kind of mortal form’ (Empedocles, fragment 115) — we must therefore believe that they have been handed over to certain keepers of this prison.”

See how here too he wavers, as a man will, over so many questions, and by setting out the opinions of several thinkers on the cause of our coming into being he shows a certain caution, not daring to declare any one of them false. Would it not, then, have befitted such a man, once he had resolved neither to assent at random nor boldly to set aside the views of the ancients, at least to doubt, if he did not wish to believe, about the teaching of the Jews set forth in their prophets and about Jesus? Would it not have befitted him to consider that it was likely that those who served the God of all, and who for the sake of honour toward him and toward what they believed he had laid down as law often accepted countless dangers and deaths, were not overlooked by God, but that some manifestation came to them also, since they had disdained the works of human art in statues and tried to ascend by reason to the God over all himself?

He ought to have considered that the common Father and Creator of all, who sees all things and hears all things, judges according to its worth the choice of each person that seeks him and wishes to be devout, and grants to these also some fruit of his protection, so that they may further increase the conception of him which they have once received. For if Celsus had reasoned this out, and with him those who hate Moses and the prophets among the Jews, and Jesus, and his genuine disciples who wore themselves out for the sake of his word, they would not have heaped such abuse on Moses and the prophets and Jesus and his apostles. Nor would they have rejected the Jews alone of all the nations on earth, saying that they were worse even than the Egyptians, who, as far as lay in them, brought the honour paid to the divine down even to irrational animals, whether from superstition or for whatever other cause or error.

We have said this not to urge anyone to doubt about the Christian teaching, but to show that for those who revile the teaching of Christians in every way it would be better at least to doubt about these matters, and not to speak so rashly about Jesus or his disciples. For they speak of things they do not know, and they make their declarations without what the Stoics call the cognitive impression and without any other criterion; and on the criterion each school of philosophers has argued for its own view, as it thought best.

title: The prisoners whom Jesus sets free
english: Then, since Celsus says, “We must therefore believe that they are handed over to certain keepers of this prison,” we must answer him that a virtuous soul is set free from the bonds of wickedness even while it is still in the life of those whom Jeremiah called “prisoners of the earth” (Lamentations 3:34). It is set free thanks to Jesus, who spoke as the prophet Isaiah foretold long before his coming. And what did Isaiah foretell him as saying, if not, “To the prisoners, Come out, and to those in darkness, Be brought to light” (Isaiah 49:9)? This is indeed Jesus, as the same Isaiah foretold of him: “On those sitting in the region and shadow of death a light has dawned” (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16). And so, because of this, we say, “Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke away from us” (Psalm 2:3).

If Celsus, and those who are set against us as he is, could hear the depth of the Gospels, he would not have advised us to obey those he called keepers of the prison. It is written in the Gospel that a certain woman “was bent double and unable to straighten herself fully” (Luke 13:11). When Jesus saw her, and saw why she was bent double, not being allowed to straighten herself “fully”, he said, “And this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan bound for eighteen long years, ought she not to have been loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13:16). How many others now, bound by Satan, are bent double, unable because of him to “straighten themselves fully”, since he wants us to look downward? And no one sets them upright except the Word who came to dwell in Jesus, and who also inspired men before that. Jesus came to set free “all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10:38). And of the devil he said, with a depth befitting him, “Now the ruler of this world has been judged” (John 16:11; John 12:31).

We do not, then, revile the demons here on earth; rather, we expose their workings for the destruction of the human race. Under the pretext of oracles, of healing bodies, and of certain other things, they seek to separate from God the soul that has fallen into “the body of humiliation” (Philippians 3:21). Those who have understood the soul so fallen cry aloud, “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

Yet we do not offer our bodies to be racked and beaten to death without reason. For the one who is plotted against by the demons and by those who worship them, because he will not let the earthly demons be proclaimed gods, does not give up his body to these things without reason. And we have rightly held that it is pleasing to God to be beaten to death for virtue, to be racked for piety, and to die for holiness. For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones” (Psalm 116:15). And we say that it is good, too, not to cling to life.

Celsus likens us to criminals, who deservedly endure what they suffer for robbery; and, showing no reverence for so great a purpose, he declares it to be like the disposition of robbers. In this he makes himself a brother of those who reckoned Jesus “among the lawless”, in whose case the scripture was fulfilled that says, “He was reckoned among the lawless” (Isaiah 53:12; Mark 15:28; Luke 22:37).

title: Celsus’s two choices
english: Next Celsus says: “Reason makes us choose one of two courses. If they refuse to give the overseers of these things the service that befits them, then they should neither take a husband nor take a wife nor raise children nor do anything else in life, but depart from here one and all, leaving no seed behind, so that such a race might be wholly wiped out from the earth. But if they are going to take wives and have children and taste the fruits and share in the things of life and bear the evils appointed for them — for this is the way of nature, that all men experience evils; for evils must exist, and they have no other place (see Plato, Theaetetus 176a) — then they must render the fitting honours to those who have been entrusted with these things, and perform the duties that befit life until they are released from their bonds, so that they may not also seem ungrateful toward these beings. For it is unjust to share in what they possess and contribute nothing to them.”

To this too we say that no departure from life seems reasonable to us except that alone which is for the sake of piety and virtue: when those who are thought to sit as judges, or who seem to have power over our life, set before us one of two things, either to live while doing what is contrary to the commands of Jesus, or to die while obeying his words.

But God has also allowed us to marry, since not all can receive what is better, that is, complete purity (Matthew 19:11); and he has charged those who marry to rear without fail what is born to them, and not to destroy the children given by providence. And this does not conflict with our refusal to obey the demons who have the earth as their domain; for, armed with the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:11), we stand as athletes of piety against the race of demons that plot against us.

title: God or mammon
english: So even if, by his own argument, Celsus sends us one and all out of life, so that, as he thinks, such a race of ours may be wholly wiped out from the earth, we for our part will live among the works of the One who created us, according to the laws of God, in no way willing to be slaves to the laws of sin (Romans 7:25). And we will marry, if we wish, and receive the children given to us in our marriages. And if need be, we will share in the things of life, bearing the appointed evils as trials of the soul. For this is what the divine words usually call what befalls men; and in these the soul of man, tested like gold in the fire, is either exposed or shown to be admirable (1 Peter 1:6–7; Sirach 2:5).

And we are so prepared for what Celsus calls evils that we even say, “Test me, Lord, and try me; put my inmost parts and my heart to the fire” (Psalm 26:2). For no one “is crowned unless he competes according to the rules” (2 Timothy 2:5) here on earth, with “the body of humiliation” (Philippians 3:21).

Moreover, we do not render the honours thought to be due to those to whom, Celsus says, the things here have been entrusted. For we worship “the Lord” our “God” and serve “him alone” (Matthew 4:10), praying to become imitators of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). When the devil said to him, “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9), he answered, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10). That is why we do not render the honours thought fitting to those to whom, Celsus says, the things here have been entrusted: because “no one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24), and we cannot at once “serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24), whether that name belongs to one being or to many.

Further, if anyone dishonours the lawgiver “through transgression of the law” (Romans 2:23), it seems clear to us that, when two laws stand opposed to each other, the law of God and the law of mammon, it is better for us to dishonour mammon “through transgression of the law” of mammon, so that by keeping the law of God we may honour God, than to dishonour God “through transgression of the law” of God, so that by keeping the law of mammon we may honour mammon.

title: Thanks due to God, not to demons
english: Celsus, then, thinks that men perform the duties that befit life, until they are released from their bonds, when they render the sacrifices, according to the customs of the many, to each of the gods recognized in each city. He has not understood what exact piety takes to be truly fitting. We, however, say that the one who performs what befits life is the one who remembers who the Creator is and what is pleasing to him, and who does all things in order to please God.

And again, Celsus does not want us to be ungrateful toward the demons here, since he thinks we owe them thank-offerings. But we, setting out clearly the teaching on thanksgiving, say that we do nothing ungrateful toward beings who do us no good but, on the contrary, stand against us, when we do not sacrifice to them, nor even serve them. What we guard against is being ungrateful toward God, whose benefits fill us. We are his creatures, cared for by him in whatever state his judgment has placed us, and beyond this life we look for the hopes that come from him. And we have a token of our thanksgiving to God: the bread called “Eucharist”, that is, “Thanksgiving”.

Nor, as we said above as well, do demons have the management of the things created for our needs. Therefore we do nothing unjust when we partake of created things and do not sacrifice to those to whom they do not belong. And if we perceive that it is not some demons but angels who are set over the fruits of the earth and the birth of living creatures, we speak well of them and call them blessed, since God has entrusted them with what is useful to our race. Yet we do not give them the honour owed to God; for neither does God wish this, nor do those entrusted with such tasks themselves. Indeed, they welcome us more when we refrain from sacrificing to them than if we sacrificed; for they have no need of the fumes that rise from the earth.

title: Celsus and the thirty-six Egyptian demons
english: After this Celsus says words to this effect: “That in these matters, down to the very least, there is someone to whom authority has been given, one may learn from what the Egyptians say. They say that thirty-six demons, or certain ethereal gods, have divided the human body among them, apportioned into that many parts (some say far more), and each has been charged to tend a different part of it. They also know the names of the demons in their native tongue, such as Chnoumen, Chnachoumen, Knat, Sikat, Biou, Erou, Erebiou, Ramanor and Reianoor, and all the others they name in their own language; and by calling on them they heal the ailments of the parts. What then prevents anyone who so wishes from paying his respects to these and to the others, and so being healthy rather than sick, fortunate rather than unfortunate, and set free, as far as possible, from tortures and punishments?”

With these words Celsus tries to drag our soul down to the demons, as though they had received our bodies as their allotted portion, and he declares that each one presides over a part of our body. He wants us to trust the demons he speaks of and to serve them, so that we may be healthy rather than sick, fortunate rather than unfortunate, and be released from tortures to the full extent that it can be done. Yet so low is his opinion of the whole and undivided honour paid to the God of all that he does not believe that God alone, worshipped and honoured with a loud voice, is enough to give the one who honours Him, from the very act of revering Him, a power that holds back the plots of the demons against the devout. For he has not seen how the invocation of the name of Jesus by those who truly believe has healed not a few people from diseases, from possession by demons, and from other afflictions.

title: The name of Jesus against the Egyptian list
english: Probably the one who embraces Celsus’s views will laugh when we say that “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue” is brought “to confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10–11). But once he has laughed, he will receive more effective proofs that this is so than any he has about the names he reports, Chnoumen, Chnachoumen, Knat, Sikat and the rest of the Egyptian list, on the claim that, when invoked, they heal the ailments of the parts.

And see how, while turning us away from believing in the God of all through Jesus Christ, he calls us, for the healing of our body, to faith in thirty-six barbarian demons, whom only the Egyptian magicians invoke, promising us, I do not know how, better things. So, according to Celsus, it is time for us to practise trickery and sorcery rather than to be Christians, and to believe in some countless number of demons rather than in the God over all, who is evident at once, living and plain to see, believing in Him through the One who with great power sowed the pure word of godliness over the whole inhabited world of men, and, I shall not lie if I add it, over the world of the other rational beings too, who also need correction, healing and a change away from wickedness.

title: Celsus’s own warning against demon worship
english: Celsus, at any rate, suspected that those who have learned such things slide into magic, and he somehow sensed that harm would come to those who heard them. So he says: “One must, however, guard against this: that no one, by keeping company with these beings, should be wholly absorbed in their worship, and, coming to love the body and turning away from higher things, be held fast by forgetfulness. For perhaps we ought not to disbelieve wise men, who say that most of the earthly demons are fused with the world of becoming, nailed to blood and the smoke of sacrifice and to songs, and bound to other such things, and could do nothing better than heal a body and foretell the coming fortune of a man and of a city; and all that concerns mortal affairs, this they know and can do.”

Since the danger of slipping in this matter is so great, as even the enemy bears witness to the truth of God, how much better it is, free from any fear of being absorbed into such demons, or of loving the body, turning away from higher things and being held fast by forgetfulness of higher things, to entrust oneself to the God over all through Jesus Christ, who gave us such teaching, and to ask from Him all help and the protection of holy angels and of the righteous, so that they may rescue us from the earthly demons. These are fused with the world of becoming, nailed to blood and the smoke of sacrifice, drawn by outlandish songs and bound to other such things, and, as even Celsus admits, can do nothing better than heal the body.

But I would say that it is not even clear that these demons, however they are served, can heal bodies. Rather, if a person wishes to live in a simpler and more ordinary way, he should see to the healing of the body by medical means; but if he wishes to live better than the many, by piety toward the God over all and by prayers to Him.

title: Which worshipper God accepts
english: Consider for yourself too: which character will the God over all more readily accept, He who has power as no one else has, for all things and for doing good to men, whether in soul or in body or in outward things? Will it be the one devoted to Him in all things, or the one who busies himself with the names of demons, their powers and workings, with spells and herbs suited to demons, with stones and the carvings on them, made to match the forms of demons that have been handed down, whether symbolic or of some other kind?

It is clear to anyone who can follow the argument even a little that the character free of pretence and free of curious arts, and for that very reason devoted to the God over all, will be acceptable to God and to all who are His own. But the character that, for the sake of bodily health, love of the body and good fortune in things that are neither good nor bad, busies itself with the names of demons and seeks how it may charm the demons with certain spells, God will leave, as wicked, impious and more demonic than human, to the demons chosen by the man who addresses such words to them, to be torn apart by the thoughts each of them suggests, or by other evils as well.

For it is likely that, being base, and, as Celsus admitted, nailed to blood and the smoke of sacrifice and to songs and other such things, they do not keep faith, or their pledges, so to speak, even toward those who gratify them with these things. For when others call on them against those who have served them, and buy their service with more blood and smoke of sacrifice and the worship they crave, they would plot against the man who served them yesterday and gave them a share of the feast they love.

title: Celsus admits what Christians say of oracles
english: Earlier Celsus said a great deal, going so far as to speak of oracles and to send us off to their oracular shrines as though to gods. Now he has done better, admitting that those who foretell the coming fortune of a man and of a city, and all who are concerned with mortal affairs, are earthly demons, fused with the world of becoming, nailed to blood and the smoke of sacrifice and to songs, and bound to other such things, and able to do nothing better than these.

And it is likely that, when we were standing against Celsus as he treated the oracles and the worship given to the supposed gods as divine, someone took us for impious, because we said that these were the works of demons who drag the souls of men down to the affairs of the world of becoming. But now let the one who formed that opinion of us be persuaded that what Christians proclaim is well said, seeing that even the man who writes against Christians has now, at the end, put this in writing, as though overcome by the Spirit of truth (John 14:17).

So even if Celsus says: “We must pay these their due rites, so far as it is to our advantage, for reason does not justify doing this in every respect,” we must not pay due rites to demons that are fused with the smoke of sacrifice and with blood, nor must we, for our part, defile the divine by dragging it down to wicked demons. If Celsus had examined the idea of advantage with care and had seen that what is advantage in the proper sense is virtue and action in keeping with virtue, he would not have set down “so far as it is to our advantage” in the case of beings like these, who are, as he himself admitted, demons.

We therefore choose, if health and good fortune in the affairs of life are to come to us through the worship of such demons, rather to be sick and to be unfortunate in the affairs of life, with a conscience that is purely reverent toward the God of all, than to be healthy in body and to fare more fortunately in the affairs of life while being cut off and falling away from God and being sick in soul to the last degree and wretched. We must draw near to Him who needs nothing at all except the salvation of men and of every rational being, rather than to those who crave the smoke of sacrifice and blood.

title: Celsus recants and urges courting rulers
english: Celsus, I think, after all the words he spoke about demons who need the smoke of sacrifice and blood, as though turning to wickedness, sings a recantation and says that “we should rather believe that the demons need nothing and lack nothing, but take pleasure in those who act piously toward them.” If he thought this was true, he ought not to have set down those earlier words; he should have struck them out.

But human nature is not wholly abandoned by God and by the Truth, His only-begotten. That is why Celsus too spoke the truth in what he said about the smoke of sacrifice and the blood that demons crave; but again, by his own wickedness, he slid down into falsehood, and he likens the demons to men who do what is just in a perfectly just way, even if no one thanks them, and who do good to those who repay them with gratitude.

He seems to me to be confused on this subject: at one moment his ruling mind is troubled by the demons, and at another, coming back to his senses from the folly he suffers under them, he sees a little of the truth. For again he adds: “But God must not be forsaken anywhere or in any way, neither by day nor by night, neither in public nor in private, in every word and in every deed continually; indeed, both with these and apart from them, let the soul be always directed toward God.” I take “with these” to mean with public life, with every deed and with every word.

Then again, as though wrestling in his reasoning against the frenzies that come from the demons and being mostly overcome, he goes on to say: “If this is so, what is so dreadful in winning the favour of the rulers here, both the others and the princes and kings among men, since not even these have been granted their place in this world without the strength of demons?” Earlier, as far as it lay with him, he was dragging our soul down to the demons; now he wants us to win the favour of the princes and kings among men as well. Since life and the histories are full of examples of these men, I have not thought it necessary to set them out now.

title: Seek the favour of the one God
english: So it is the one God over all whose favour we must seek, and we must pray to Him to be gracious; His favour is won by piety and by every virtue. But if Celsus wants us to win the favour of some others too, after the God over all, let him consider this: just as the movement of its shadow follows a body in motion, in the same way, winning the favour of the God over all brings with it the goodwill of all His friends, angels and souls and spirits.

For they perceive who are worthy of favour from God, and not only do they themselves become well disposed to the worthy, but they also work together with those who wish to serve the God over all; they seek His favour for them, they pray with them and join in their requests. So we dare to say that when men who by deliberate choice set the better things before them pray to God, countless holy powers pray with them unbidden. They stand by our mortal race and, if I may put it so, share its struggle and anguish, because they see the demons waging war and contending against salvation, most of all the salvation of those who dedicate themselves to God and take no thought of the hatred of the demons, if the demons grow savage against the man who flees their worship with the smoke of sacrifice and blood, and who by every manner of word and deed hastens to be made kin to the God over all and united with Him through Jesus, who overthrew countless demons when He went about “healing” and turning back “those who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10:38).

title: Obedience to rulers, but no oath by the emperor’s fortune
english: We, however, must scorn to win the favour of men and kings, not only if we would win it by murders, by debauchery and by the most savage deeds, but also if we would win it by impiety toward the God of the universe, or by any word spoken with servility and abjectness. Such words are foreign to brave and great-souled men, who wish to take up endurance, as the greatest of virtues, together with the other virtues. Yet where we do nothing contrary to the law and word of God, we are not mad, nor are we eager to rouse against ourselves the anger of a king or a ruler, which would bring us to outrages and tortures, or even to death. For we have also read: “Let every soul be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been appointed by God; so whoever resists the authority resists what God has ordained” (Romans 13:1–2).

In our commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans we examined these words too, more fully and from various sides, as far as we were able. Here we have taken them more simply, according to the more common interpretation, to suit the matter in hand, since Celsus says: “Not even these men have been granted the things of this world without the power of demons.” And since the subject of the appointment of kings and rulers is a large one, and the passage raises much inquiry because of those who have ruled with cruelty and tyranny, or those who, once in power, have run aground on softness and luxury, we have for that reason put off examining the problem for the present.

We do not, however, swear by the fortune of the emperor, any more than by any other supposed god. For if, as some have put it, fortune is only a way of speaking, like “seeming” and “distance,” then we do not swear by what does not exist at all as though it were a god, or as though it had any real existence and could do anything, so that we may not apply the power of an oath where it ought not to be applied. Or if, as some have held when they say, “Those who swear by the fortune of the Roman emperor swear by his demon,” what is called the emperor’s fortune is a demon, then in that case we must rather die than swear by a wicked and faithless demon, which often sins along with the man to whom it was allotted, or even sins more than he does.

title: Hymns to the Sun and to Athena
english: Then again Celsus, like those who at times recover from demonic possession and then fall back again, says something like this, as though he were sober: “If, however, someone should command one who happens to worship God either to act impiously or to say anything else shameful, he must in no way at all be obeyed; rather than this, one must endure every torture and submit to every kind of death, before one would even think, let alone say, anything unholy about God.” Then again, out of ignorance of our teaching, and besides that because he jumbles everything together, he says this: “But if someone commands you to praise the Sun or Athena, praise them with the utmost eagerness in a fine hymn; in this way you will seem all the more to worship the great God, if you hymn these too; for piety becomes more complete when it passes through all things.”

We answer, then, that we do not wait for someone to command us before we praise the sun, we who have learned to speak well not only of those who are subject to God’s ordering but even of our enemies (compare Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28). So we praise the sun as a fine work of God, which keeps the laws of God and hears the words, “Praise the Lord, sun and moon” (Psalm 148:3), and which with all its power hymns the Father and Creator of the universe.

As for Athena, however, whom the accounts of the Greeks set beside the sun, they made her the subject of myth, saying, whether with hidden meanings or without them, that she was born fully armed from the head of Zeus; and that once, when Hephaestus pursued her in the wish to destroy her virginity, she escaped him, but that she loved the seed which fell to the earth from his lust and reared it, calling it Erichthonius, “whom once,” they say, “Athena, daughter of Zeus, reared, but the grain-giving earth bore” (Homer, Iliad 2.547–548). And we see that one who accepts Athena, the daughter of Zeus, must accept with her many myths and fictions, which one who flees from myths and seeks the truth would not accept.

title: We hymn only God and His Word
english: Even if Athena is allegorised and said to be wisdom, let someone establish her real existence and her substance, showing that she subsists in the way this allegory says. And if Athena was once a woman of ancient times and has been honoured because those who wished her name to be sung among men as a goddess handed down mysteries and rites to their subjects, then all the more ought we not to hymn Athena and glorify her as a goddess, since it is not lawful for us even to worship the sun, great as it is, though we praise it.

Celsus, then, says that we seem the more to worship the great God if we hymn both the Sun and Athena; but we know the opposite. For we sing hymns only to the God over all and to His only-begotten, God the Word (compare John 1:1; John 1:18). And we hymn God and His Only-begotten, as do also “sun and moon” and “stars” (Psalm 148:3) and the whole heavenly host (compare Luke 2:13). For all these, being a divine choir, together with the righteous among men, hymn the God over all and His Only-begotten.

We said before that we must not swear by the king among men, or by what is called his fortune. So we need not defend ourselves again against this: “And even if someone commands you to take an oath by a king among men, not even this is anything terrible. For to him have been given the things on earth, and whatever you receive in this life, you receive from him.” But we say that it is by no means true that all things on earth have been given to him, nor do we receive from him whatever we receive in this life. For whatever we receive justly and rightly, we receive from God and His providence: cultivated crops, and bread that “strengthens the heart of man,” and the gentle vine, and wine that “gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15). The fruit of the olive too we have from the providence of God, “to make the face shine with oil” (Psalm 104:15).

title: One king, appointed by God and not by the son of Cronus
english: Next Celsus says that one must not disbelieve an ancient man who long ago declared: “One king, to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave it” (Homer, Iliad 2.205). And he adds: “For if you overthrow this teaching, the king will rightly punish you. For if all were to do the same as you, nothing would prevent him from being left alone and deserted, and the affairs of the earth from falling into the hands of the most lawless and savage barbarians, and nothing would keep the fame of your religion, or of the true wisdom, from vanishing from among men.”

Let there be, then, “one lord, one king” (Homer, Iliad 2.204–205); not one “to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave it,” but one to whom He gave it who “sets up kings and removes them” (Daniel 2:21) and at the right time raises up “the man who is useful” over the earth (Sirach 10:4). And it is not the son of Cronus who appoints kings, the son who drove from his rule the father who, as the myths of the Greeks say, was cast down into Tartarus; nor is it so even if someone allegorises what is said in those passages. Rather, God who governs all things knows what He is doing in the matter of the appointment of kings.

We do overthrow, then, the teaching “to whom the son of crooked-counselling Cronus gave it,” since we are persuaded that neither a god nor a father of a god wills anything crooked or twisted. But we do not overthrow the teaching about providence, and about the things that come about by it either as its primary purpose or as consequences that follow from certain other things. Nor would a king rightly punish us for saying that it was not the son of crooked-counselling Cronus who gave him his kingship, but He who “removes kings and sets them up” (Daniel 2:21).

Yes, let all do the same as I do, overthrowing the Homeric teaching while keeping the divine teaching about the king and observing the words, “Honour the king” (1 Peter 2:17). On such a supposition the king will not be left alone, nor will he be deserted, nor will the affairs of the earth fall to the most lawless and savage barbarians. For if, as Celsus says, all were to do the same as I do, clearly the barbarians too, when they come to the Word of God, will be most law-abiding and most gentle; and every religion will be abolished, and that of the Christians alone will prevail. And indeed it alone will one day prevail, since the Word is always winning more and more souls.

title: If the Romans prayed with one accord
english: Then Celsus, not hearing himself as he says things that do not hang together in the words, “For if all were to do the same as you,” says: “Surely you will not say this: that if the Romans, persuaded by you, were to neglect their customary duties toward gods and men and call upon your Most High, or whoever you like, he will come down and fight for them, and they will need no other help. For before this too the same God, as you say, promised these things and far greater ones to those who gave heed to him; and you see how much he has helped both them and you. Of them, instead of their being masters of the whole earth, not so much as a clod of soil or a hearth is left; and of you, if any still wanders about in hiding, yet he is hunted down to be punished with death.”

But since he asks, by way of supposition, what would happen if the Romans, persuaded by the doctrine of the Christians, were to neglect their duties toward the customary gods and the former laws among men and worship the Most High, hear what we hold about this. We say that if “two” of us “agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by the Father” of the righteous, “who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:19) — for God rejoices in the concord of rational beings and turns away from discord — what must we think if not only a very few, as now, were to agree, but the whole empire under the Romans? For they will pray to the Word who said long ago to the Hebrews when the Egyptians were pursuing them: “The Lord will fight for you, and you shall keep silent” (Exodus 14:14). And praying in complete concord they will be able to destroy far more enemies who pursue them than those whom the prayer of Moses and of those with him brought down, when he cried out to God (compare Exodus 14:15).

If the things that God promised to those who keep the law have not come about, they have failed to come about not because God lies, but because the promises were made on conditions, the conditions of keeping the law and living according to the law. And if neither clod nor hearth is left to the Jews, who received the promises on conditions, the blame must be laid on all their transgression of the law, and above all on their transgression against Jesus.

title: Christians are the salt that preserves the world
english: But on Celsus’s supposition, if all the Romans were persuaded, by praying they will overcome their enemies, or they will not even make war at all, guarded by the divine power which promised to save five whole cities for the sake of fifty righteous men (compare Genesis 18:24–26). For the men of God are salt that preserves the order of the world on earth, and the things on earth hold together as long as the salt does not go bad. For “if the salt has lost its taste,” it “is no longer fit either for the soil or for the dunghill,” but “is thrown out” and will be trampled “by men” (Matthew 5:13; Luke 14:34–35). “He who has ears, let him hear” (Luke 14:35) how these things are said.

We too, when God allows the tempter and gives him authority to persecute us, are persecuted; but when God does not wish us to suffer this, even in a world that hates us (compare John 15:18) we live in peace, against all expectation, and take courage from Him who said: “Take courage, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). And truly He has overcome “the world”; therefore the world has power only so far as He who overcame it wills, since He received from the Father the power to overcome “the world.” And we take courage from His victory.

But if He wishes us once more to contend and struggle for piety, let the adversaries come, and we will say to them: “I can do all things in Him who strengthens me, Christ Jesus our Lord” (Philippians 4:13; 1 Timothy 1:12). For when two sparrows are sold “for a penny,” as Scripture names the price, “not one falls into a snare without the Father in heaven” (Matthew 10:29). And divine providence has embraced all things so fully that not even the hairs “of our head” have escaped being numbered by Him (Matthew 10:30).

title: Celsus invents a claim no Christian made
english: Then again, as is his habit, Celsus muddles things together in what follows, saying what none of us has ever written. For he says something like this: “Nor is it tolerable when you say that, if those who now reign over us are persuaded by you and are taken captive, you will persuade those who reign after them, then others, if they too are taken, and others after others, until, when all who are persuaded by you are being taken, some one government, coming to its senses and foreseeing what is happening, will wipe you all out, race and all, before it is itself destroyed.”

There is no call to speak about this, for none of us says about those who now reign that, if they are persuaded and are taken, we will in turn persuade those after them, and when those are taken we will again persuade the next. And where did he get the idea he has thrown out here, that, as later rulers are always persuaded by us in succession and are taken because they do not defend themselves against the enemy, some one government, coming to its senses and foreseeing what is happening, will wipe us out, race and all? It seems rather that here, stringing one piece of nonsense onto another, he has also blurted this out from his own head.

title: Can all rational beings agree under one law?
english: After this he utters a kind of wish: “If only it were possible for the Greeks and barbarians who inhabit Asia, Europe and Libya, to their farthest bounds, to come to agreement under one law!” Then, judging this impossible, he adds that “whoever thinks this knows nothing.”

If something must be said on this too, a few things will be said on the subject, though it needs much examination and proof, to show that what is said about every rational being coming to agree under one law is not only possible but true. The Stoics say that when the element which is stronger than the others has prevailed, as far as it can, the conflagration will come, with all things changing into fire. But we say that the Word will one day gain mastery over the whole of rational nature and transform every soul into his own perfection, when each one, using nothing but his own freedom, chooses what he wills and comes to be in what he has chosen.

And we say that it is not reasonable to think that, as with diseases and wounds in the body some of the things that happen prove stronger than the whole art of medicine, so with souls some effect of wickedness cannot be healed by the Word, who is over all and is God. For the Word is mightier than all the evils in the soul, and so is the healing that is in him, and he applies it to each one according to the will of God; and the end of things is that wickedness be destroyed. Whether it will be destroyed so that it can never again, anywhere or in any way, be permitted, or not, it is not the task of the present discussion to teach.

Now the prophecies say many things, in veiled terms, about the complete destruction of evils and the setting right of every soul; for the present it is enough to set out the passage from Zephaniah, which runs thus: “Make ready, rise early: all their gleaning is ruined. Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my rising up for a testimony; for my judgment is upon the gatherings of the nations, to receive kings, to pour out upon them all the wrath of my anger. For in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be consumed. For then I will turn for the peoples a tongue into its own generation, so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke. From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia they shall offer sacrifices to me. On that day you shall not be put to shame for all your practices by which you acted impiously against me; for then I will take away from you the contemptible things of your insolence, and you shall no longer go on boasting upon my holy mountain. And I will leave in you a people meek and lowly, and the remnant of Israel shall reverence the name of the Lord; and they shall do no wrong and speak no vain things, and no deceitful tongue shall be found in their mouth; for they shall feed and lie down, and there shall be no one to make them afraid” (Zephaniah 3:7–13).

Let anyone who is able, having studied all of this, set out the clear meaning of the prophecy; and let him examine above all what it means that, when all the earth is being consumed, a tongue is turned “for the peoples into its own generation” (Zephaniah 3:9), in a way that answers to the state of things before the confusion (Genesis 11:7–9). And let him consider what it means for “all to call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke” (Zephaniah 3:9), so that “the contemptible things of insolence” are taken away (Zephaniah 3:11), and there is no longer “wrong,” nor vain words, nor a deceitful tongue (Zephaniah 3:13).

I have thought it right to set these things out briefly and without a precise exposition, because of Celsus’s statement, since he thinks it impossible for the Greeks and barbarians who live in Asia, Europe and Libya to come to agreement. And perhaps such a thing truly is impossible for those who are still in bodies, but not impossible for those who have been set free from them.

title: Christians help the emperor by prayer
english: Next Celsus urges us to help the emperor with all our strength, to labour with him in what is just, to fight for him, to serve in his army if he presses us, and to share command with him.

To this too we must say that we do help emperors when there is need, with a help that is, so to speak, divine, and taking up “the whole armour of God” (Ephesians 6:13). And we do this in obedience to the apostle’s voice, which says: “I urge you, then, first to make petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). And the more pious a person is, the more effective he is in helping those who reign: more effective than the soldiers who go out to the battle lines and kill as many of the enemy as they can.

Then we might also say this to those who are strangers to the faith and who demand that we serve as soldiers for the common good and kill men: even among you, the priests of certain images and the temple-keepers of those you consider gods keep their right hands undefiled for the sake of the sacrifices, so that they may offer the customary sacrifices to those you call gods with hands free of blood and clean of killing; and surely, when war comes, you do not enlist the priests too. If, then, this is reasonably done, how much more reasonably, while others go to war, do these also wage their war as priests and servants of God, keeping their right hands clean but striving through prayers to God for those who fight in a just cause and for him who reigns justly, so that everything opposed and hostile to those who act justly may be overthrown?

And we, by our prayers overthrowing all the demons who stir up wars, break oaths and disturb peace, help those who reign more than those who seem to be soldiers do. We share the labours of public affairs, we who offer up prayers with righteousness, together with disciplines and meditations that teach us to despise pleasures and not to be led by them. We fight for the emperor even more; and we do not serve in his army, even if he presses us, but we wage war on his behalf, raising an army of our own, an army of piety, through our intercessions to the Deity.

title: How Christians lead for their country
english: And if Celsus wants us to lead armies for our country as well, let him know that we do this too, and not so as to be seen by men or to win empty glory from them by doing it (Matthew 6:1). For in our secret place, in the very ruling part of the soul, prayers are sent up, as from priests, for those in our country (Matthew 6:6).

Christians do more good to their countries than the rest of mankind. They educate the citizens and teach them to be devout toward God, the guardian of the city, and they take up into a divine and heavenly city those who have lived well in the least of cities. To them it might be said: in a very small city “you were faithful” (Luke 19:17); come also to the great one, where “God has taken his stand in the assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges gods” (Psalm 82:1), and he numbers you too among them, if you no longer die like a man nor fall “like one of the rulers” (Psalm 82:7).

title: Why Christians govern churches rather than cities
english: Celsus also urges us to take office in our country, if this too must be done for the sake of preserving the laws and piety. But we know that in each city there is another organised country, founded by the Word of God, and we call those who are able to govern, sound in word and in life, to govern churches. We do not accept those who love to rule, but we press those who, out of great modesty, do not wish to take on hastily the common care of the church of God. And those who rule well among us are men who were pressed into it, compelled by the great King, whom we are persuaded is the Son of God, God the Word.

And if those who rule well in the church rule over the country that is according to God (I mean the Church), whether asked or pressed, they rule according to what God has commanded, and in doing so they defile none of the laws that have been laid down. And it is not to escape the more common public duties of life that Christians avoid such offices, but to keep themselves for a more divine and more necessary service, that of the church of God, for the salvation of men. In this service they lead both of necessity and with justice, and they take thought for all: for those within, that they may live better day by day; and for those who seem to be outside, that they may come to be within the holy words and works of godliness, and so, worshipping God truly and teaching many as far as they can, may be blended with the Word of God and the divine law, and thus be united to the God over all through the Son of God, who is Word, Wisdom, Truth and Righteousness, and who unites to him everyone who has been moved to live in all things according to God.

title: Closing words to Ambrose
english: With this, holy Ambrose, you have the completion of what you charged us to do, carried out with the power that we have and that was given to us. In eight books we have set down everything that we thought it fitting to dictate in answer to Celsus’s book entitled The True Doctrine. It is for the one who reads his treatise, and what we dictated against it, to judge which of the two breathes more of the true God, of the way of piety toward Him, and of the truth that reaches to men, the truth of sound doctrines that urge them on to the best life.

Know, however, that Celsus announces that he will write another treatise after this one, in which he promised to teach how those who wish to follow him, and are able to, ought to live. If, then, he did not write the second book, though he promised it, it would be well for us to be content with the eight books dictated in answer to his treatise. But if he began that one too and completed it, search for the work and send it, so that, dictating in answer to it also whatever the Father of truth may give us, we may overturn the false belief it contains, and, if something true is said anywhere, may bear witness to it without contention as something well said.
